# Welcome {-}

How many patients would you need to compare a new pain treatment with standard treatment? This tutorial helps you justify a sample size that can answer your research question, using clinical examples, calculations and simulation.

Although the examples are clinical, the principles of justifying assumptions, choosing a target difference, and examining power and precision also apply in psychology, education, and other quantitative disciplines [@lakens2022]. The tutorial is a suitable starting point for learning these principles and planning comparisons of two independent groups with a continuous or binary outcome, provided the calculation’s assumptions match your study. Later chapters introduce other planning goals and help you recognize when a different method is needed. For factorial experiments and repeated-measures ANOVA, including designs common in psychology, *[Power Analysis with Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/)* provides more directly applicable examples and simulations [@superpowerbook2022]. Studies involving multilevel models, prediction, or time-to-event outcomes need guidance matched to those analyses; [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) points you toward relevant resources. What counts as a worthwhile difference should also reflect your field and research question.

## How to use this tutorial {-}

This tutorial is for students and researchers. Chapters 1–4 form the Core route for basic two-arm trial planning. Chapters 5–9 offer Advanced topics that you can consult according to your study question. The glossary and common questions are reference pages for either route.

Activities are learning exercises. Apps are the interactive software used in some activities, such as calculators, simulations and the report builder. You can record your decisions in the [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) as you read. Chapter 4 brings together the report guidance and a completed example. The same answers produce a concise sample size calculation report followed by the supporting study plan; advanced activities can extend that supporting material. Expandable misconception boxes explain common difficulties; the toolbar help explains the other reading features.

```{r tutorial-roadmap, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
roadmap <- paste(readLines("../figures/tutorial-roadmap.svg",
  encoding="UTF-8", warn=FALSE), collapse="\n")
# Numeric entities keep SVG text intact when R uses a non-UTF-8 locale.
roadmap <- paste(vapply(utf8ToInt(enc2utf8(roadmap)), function(cp) {
  if (cp > 127L) sprintf("&#%d;", cp) else intToUtf8(cp)
}, character(1)), collapse="")
cat('<figure class="tutorial-roadmap">',
    roadmap, '</figure>')
```

Each teaching chapter ends with an embedded *Check your understanding* quiz. The material comes together in a [cumulative quiz](#cumulative-quiz).

You can open [the tutorial and an app together](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many), consult the [activity walkthroughs](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/activity-walkthroughs.html), or review terms in the [Glossary](#glossary). For your own project, [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) helps you choose an approach. Its advanced section on [units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis) explains how grouping and paired measurements affect the information a study provides.

[Flashcards](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/index.html) are available for Core and Core + Advanced, with a [question-and-answer preview](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/student-materials/flashcards/cards.html) and Anki/Quizlet downloads. Questions and suggestions are welcome through [Feedback](https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/j00AMibqi5).

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
## Core learning outcomes {#core-route .unnumbered .core-heading}

The linked sections should help you develop a sample size justification for a basic two-arm trial. By the end, you should be able to:

- [Define a clinical question and justify assumptions](#clinical-question), distinguishing the [difference observed in previous data](#expected-difference), [target difference](#target-difference) and [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold).
- [Explain Type I error probability, Type II error probability and power](#power).
- Use [one simulated study and many studies](#activity-1-one-study-then-many) to distinguish [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) from [population parameters](#population-parameter) and see how results vary.
- [Calculate sample size for two proportions or two means](#calculations) and [adjust recruitment for expected losses](#account-for-expected-losses), distinguishing analyzable counts from recruitment counts.
- [Examine a plausible alternative assumption](#stress-test-the-study-plan), recognize [underpowered studies](#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose) and assess [ways to increase power](#increase-power).
- [Write a short sample size justification](#write-a-sample-size-justification) recording assumptions, calculation and recruitment, using the [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question).

:::

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
## Advanced learning outcomes {#advanced-route .unnumbered .advanced-heading}

The extensions below may be relevant to your study question. They should help you:

- [Interpret confidence intervals](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) and choose a precision target for estimation.
- Distinguish [an observed significance boundary from planned power](#critical-observed-difference) and explore [sampling distributions and error regions](#alpha-beta).
- [Read power curves](#curves) and evaluate what a fixed sample can establish.
- [Build a simulated clinical trial](#simulation) to examine power, coverage and precision, accounting for [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error).
- Plan a [two-group comparison for useful precision](#plan-for-precision) or a [single-population prevalence estimate](#prevalence), matching the criterion to the research question.
- Assess [existing-data reuse](#dataset-reuse), [rare-disease constraints](#rare-diseases), and the information needed for decisions in a [pilot or feasibility study](#pilot-feasibility).
- Recognize [study designs that need another method](#study-designs), including paired measurements and prediction models.
- Explain how [multiple comparisons](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), [interim analyses](#interim-analyses-stopping) and [sample-size re-estimation](#sample-size-re-estimation) affect planning and reporting.
- [Reproduce calculations and simulations](#appendix) with their assumptions and methods documented.

:::


# Research question and power {#clinical-question .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Specify a clinical question, outcome, design and planned comparison.
- Distinguish a difference observed in earlier data, a calculation target and a clinical threshold.
- Explain Type I and Type II error probabilities and power under specified assumptions.
- Use one study and repeated studies to explain sampling variability and the effect of sample size.
:::

## The chronic pain trial: how many patients do you need? {#the-chronic-pain-study-how-many-patients-do-we-need .core-heading}

Suppose you are planning a trial of a novel pain treatment against standard treatment. Does the novel treatment increase the percentage of patients reporting pain relief at four weeks?

For this teaching case, assume that the novel treatment involves four additional clinic visits and a risk of short-lived dizziness. Both groups may continue the same background pain medication. These details will matter when judging whether an additional benefit is worthwhile.

You plan to randomly allocate patients to two [independent groups](#independent-groups) of equal size. The [primary outcome](#primary-outcome) is pain relief at four weeks: yes or no. A small [pilot study](#pilot-study) found relief in 7 of 10 patients receiving the novel treatment and 3 of 10 receiving standard treatment: 70% versus 30%, an observed difference of 40 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-pilot-patients) illustrates these pilot results.

```{r pain-pilot-patients, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.7, fig.cap="Illustration of the hypothetical pilot: ten patients per treatment group start with pain. Downward arrows lead to their outcomes at four weeks. Green figures with raised arms indicate reported pain relief; red figures indicate no reported relief at follow-up. The counts describe this small pilot sample.", fig.alt="Two treatment groups: standard treatment on the left and novel treatment on the right. Each is shown before treatment and after a downward arrow marking four weeks. All ten patients in each group start red, indicating pain. In the standard-treatment group, three of ten become green with raised arms, indicating reported pain relief, and seven remain red. In the novel-treatment group, seven of ten become green and three remain red. Pain relief is reported by 30% with standard treatment and 70% with novel treatment."}
draw_pain_pilot_patients()
```

This looks promising, but twenty patients give you limited information. How many patients would make the main trial informative? Using this example, you will calculate how many patients to recruit and explore simulated trials to see how pain-relief percentages and the difference between treatments vary from study to study.

This first section focuses on two-arm randomized superiority trials: patients are assigned by chance to one of two treatment groups, and the aim is to investigate whether one treatment performs better than the other. The core calculations cover binary and continuous outcomes. The separate [estimation chapter](#estimation-planning) uses a precision target; later chapters address other designs.

The four core chapters develop the study question, calculation, recruitment plan and final sample size calculation report. You can open the [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) at any point; [Chapter 4](#reporting) explains how to assemble and review the report.

## What should this study establish? {.core-heading}

A sample size calculation helps assess what the planned study could establish under its assumptions. With too few patients, a study may miss a clinically worthwhile difference and leave the treatment difference uncertain. Recruiting more patients than the question requires also adds participant burden and time. For the chronic pain trial, your plan should address four connected questions:

- Statistical: can the study detect a clinically worthwhile treatment difference with adequate power?
- Clinical: how much additional pain relief would matter to patients?
- Ethical: does the information the study could provide justify participants' burden and risk?
- Practical: can you recruit the required patients within the available time and recruitment capacity?

### Ethical review and the study protocol {.core-heading}

A scientifically sound study is an ethical requirement. The Declaration of Helsinki sets out international ethical principles, including scientific validity, a justified [study protocol](#study-protocol), and prior [research ethics committee](#research-ethics-committee) review [@wmahelsinki2024]. Your protocol should explain the proposed sample size, the evidence behind its assumptions, and the information expected in relation to participants' burden and risk.

For clinical trials of medicines, the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) provides a shared statistical framework used worldwide in its [E9 guideline](#ich-e9). Its sample-size guidance calls for an explicit outcome, target difference, analysis, error probabilities and assumptions, with sensitivity to uncertainty considered [@iche91998].

Review procedures depend on the country and study type. Your institution's research office or ethics committee should help identify the applicable requirements. The following are regional and national examples:

- European Union: clinical trials of medicines within the scope of Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 require scientific and ethical review; ethics committees operate under the law of the relevant member state [@ecethicsreview]. Other study types follow their applicable frameworks.
- United States: an [institutional review board (IRB)](#institutional-review-board) reviews studies subject to the relevant human-participant protections. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requirements apply to covered clinical investigations; Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) regulations apply to covered research conducted or supported by HHS [@fdairb2025; @hhsresearchreview].
- Netherlands: research within the [Medical Research Involving Human Subjects Act (WMO)](#wmo) framework is reviewed by an accredited [medical research ethics committee (METC)](#metc) or the [Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects (CCMO)](#ccmo), as applicable [@ccmowmo].

<details class="misconception" id="ethics-sample-size">
<summary>Why sample size is an ethical issue</summary>

A study should provide useful information in relation to the burdens and risks participants accept. An inadequate design may expose participants to those burdens without resolving its question; unnecessary recruitment adds avoidable burden. Scientific value, informed consent, fair recruitment, and the balance of potential benefits and harms all matter. A small feasibility study or rare-disease study may be ethically justified when its size supports a clearly defined objective. Its conclusions should match the information it can provide.

</details>

## What should you consider before calculating the sample size? {#how-do-you-determine-the-minimum-required-sample-size .core-heading}

A clear treatment-comparison question identifies the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome ([PICO](#pico){.no-glossary-tooltip}), including when the outcome is measured [@richardson1995]. Before choosing numbers, your plan should answer these general questions [@fong2026; @wang2020]:

- Who will be studied, and which intervention and comparator will be evaluated?
- What is the primary outcome, and when will it be measured?
- How will treatment be allocated?
- What population quantity will answer the question, and which analysis will estimate it and test the hypothesis?

For the chronic pain trial, the population is patients with chronic pain, the intervention is the novel treatment, the comparator is standard treatment, and the outcome is pain relief at four weeks. Patients are randomly allocated to two equally sized groups. The quantity of interest is the absolute difference between the groups' pain-relief percentages. The planned analysis compares two independent proportions and tests whether the population relief percentages differ.

Before selecting calculation inputs, you should also consult guidance for the study design. For a randomized trial, [SPIRIT](#spirit) 2025 covers the protocol and [CONSORT](#consort) 2025 covers reporting the results [@spiritconsort2025]. Other designs have corresponding guidelines, such as [STROBE](#strobe) for observational studies and [STARD](#stard) for diagnostic accuracy. These reporting guidelines identify decisions to document; [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) links to the guidance for each design.

The map below gathers the remaining decisions for the chronic pain trial. Its outcome is [binary](#binary-outcome){.no-glossary-tooltip}: each patient either reports pain relief or does not. A different question or analysis may need a different sample size method.

```{r study-questions-map, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
knitr::asis_output(render_question_map())
```

The core route uses a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test) to assess evidence of a between-group difference in either direction. The following sections explain the hypotheses, error probabilities and power needed for this calculation.

## What did the pilot show, what will you plan for, and what matters clinically? {#what-do-we-expect-what-will-we-plan-for-and-what-matters-clinically .core-heading}

The pilot result, the target difference and the clinical threshold answer three different questions. The first describes earlier observations; the other two guide the new study. All concern differences between groups.

The [difference observed in the pilot](#expected-difference){.no-glossary-tooltip} is 40 percentage points: 7 of 10 patients (70%) reported relief with novel treatment, compared with 3 of 10 (30%) with standard treatment. It summarizes these patients' outcomes. With only ten patients per group, it provides uncertain evidence about the population difference. Other studies, differences in initial pain severity, background medication, the definition of relief and assessment time should also inform the new trial's assumptions.

The [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold){.no-glossary-tooltip} is the smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile in relation to harms, burden and available alternatives. For this case, suppose patient and clinical advisers judge that at least 20 additional patients per 100 should obtain relief to justify four additional visits and the risk of short-lived dizziness. That gives a threshold of 20 percentage points. Expressing it as one additional patient with relief per five treated makes its size easier to interpret; the judgment about the burden and harms supplies the justification [@cook2018delta2].

The [target difference](#target-difference){.no-glossary-tooltip} is the assumed true difference at which the sample size calculation evaluates [power](#statistical-power). Here, you use 30 percentage points: 60% relief with novel treatment versus 30% with standard treatment. These percentages represent assumed population probabilities of relief. The smaller target asks the trial to detect a less favorable, still worthwhile benefit. Its selection remains a judgment that needs supporting evidence and calculations across plausible alternatives [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2].

The observed difference, target difference and clinical threshold may coincide and have no fixed numerical order. The observed value comes from the data; the target and threshold need a justification. These differences describe comparisons between groups; they cannot tell you how much each patient would benefit. [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) explains why.

| Quantity | Value | Role in this study |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Difference observed in the pilot | 40 percentage points: 70% versus 30% | Sample result that informs planning, with uncertainty |
| Target between-group difference | 30 percentage points: 60% versus 30% | Assumed true difference at which you evaluate power |
| Clinically worthwhile between-group difference (clinical threshold) | 20 percentage points | Smallest additional benefit judged worthwhile, considering burdens, risks, and alternatives |

Table: (\#tab:pain-planning-values) Earlier observations and two planning decisions for the chronic pain trial; their numerical values can coincide.

Figure \@ref(fig:planning-differences) places these values on the same scale. All are absolute differences in percentage points. Labels such as small, medium or large leave the clinical meaning unspecified [@caldwell2020].

An actual example is the Medical Research Council ST01 trial, which compared standard with more extensive stomach-cancer surgery. Its planners considered uncertain survival expectations alongside the additional surgical risks. The [advanced discussion of evidence and uncertainty](#st01-expectations) uses this and other studies to examine how evidence informs the calculation [@fayers2000beliefs].

```{r planning-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=3, fig.cap="Difference observed in the pilot, target difference and clinical threshold for the chronic pain trial. The pilot value is a sample result; the target and threshold concern population differences. All are expressed in percentage points. Their values may coincide or follow a different order in other studies.", fig.alt="Three compact horizontal rows share an axis for novel minus standard treatment. Each line starts at zero and ends at its labeled value: difference observed in the pilot, 40 percentage points, calculated from the pilot patients; target difference, 30 points, used to evaluate power; clinical threshold, 20 points, the smallest benefit judged worthwhile."}
draw_planning_differences()
```

A study planned for high power at 30 percentage points will generally have lower power at a 20-point difference, even though that smaller benefit matters clinically. If your main aim is to reliably detect the smallest worthwhile benefit, the target should be 20 points and the required sample will be larger. The test still assesses a difference from zero; interpreting the eventual benefit against the clinical threshold also requires its estimate and confidence interval, as the separate [estimation chapter](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) explains. Affordability alone cannot justify choosing a larger target [@cook2018delta2].

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

The plan uses a target difference of 30 percentage points. Under what circumstances would planning for 20 percentage points be more appropriate, and what would that change?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-target-choice">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Planning for 20 points would be appropriate if the study needs high power to detect the smallest benefit judged worthwhile. With the same standard-treatment percentage, Type I error probability and target power, detecting this smaller difference requires more patients. Planning for 30 points accepts a greater probability of missing a worthwhile 20-point benefit. The clinical threshold remains 20 points in either plan.

</details>
:::

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-effect">
<summary>Common misconception: the pilot reveals the true treatment effect</summary>

The pilot's observed relief percentages, 70% versus 30%, are [sample estimates](#sample-estimate) and could change in another small sample. They provide uncertain evidence about the population effect. The pilot result informs the choice of target difference alongside other evidence and clinical importance.

</details>

Small pilots can help assess recruitment and measurement procedures, but their treatment-effect estimates are uncertain [@eldridge2016]. Your planning assumptions should draw on the full relevant evidence, including less favorable findings. Selecting only promising pilot results can distort the assumptions used for the main study [@albers2018].

## Power in repeated studies {#power .core-heading}

Suppose you repeated the same planned study many times, with the same sample size, analysis and specified true treatment effect. Power is the probability that the planned test rejects the [null hypothesis](#null-hypothesis) at the specified true difference. Across repeated studies, it corresponds to the percentage detecting that difference. At 90% power, about 90 out of 100 repetitions would detect that effect if it exists, while about 10 would not. This describes the design's long-run performance. You do not need to conduct the trial repeatedly: calculations or simulations estimate this probability under the stated assumptions.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: 90% power means a 90% probability that the treatment works</summary>

Power assumes a particular true effect and describes how often the planned test would reject the null hypothesis across repeated studies. A study with 90% power can still produce an inconclusive result.

</details>

You can now return to the planning question: if pain relief is assumed to be 60% with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, how often would studies of a given size detect the difference? Power describes this repeated-study performance under the specified assumptions.

## Hypotheses and error probabilities {.core-heading}

The null hypothesis says that the population pain-relief percentages are equal. Rejecting it means that the study provides sufficient statistical evidence of a difference, using the chosen test. When the test does not reject the null hypothesis, the evidence is insufficient to establish a difference.

Let $\delta$ denote the population difference in percentages: novel treatment minus standard treatment. A positive difference favors the novel treatment; a negative difference favors standard treatment. The planned [two-sided test](#two-sided-test){.no-glossary-tooltip} asks whether this difference is zero or differs from zero in either direction. Here $H_0$ denotes the null hypothesis (no population difference), and $H_1$ denotes the alternative hypothesis (a population difference).

\begin{equation}
H_0: \delta=0, \qquad H_1: \delta\ne0.
(\#eq:hypotheses)
\end{equation}

For the sample size calculation, you assume 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment—a true difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points). Power describes how often the planned test would find a statistically significant result under that assumption. Power is calculated at the 30-point target difference. The statistical test assesses whether the population difference is zero.


```{r error-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Decision = c("Statistically significant difference (reject the null)", "No statistically significant difference (do not reject the null)"),
  `No population difference` = c("False positive (Type I error)", "True negative"),
  `Specified population difference exists` = c("True positive", "False negative (Type II error)"),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Testing decisions across repeated studies.")
```

A Type I error is a [false positive](#false-positive){.no-glossary-tooltip}: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true. The Type I error probability is the probability of falsely rejecting the null. In this trial, that means finding a statistically significant difference when the population relief probabilities are actually equal.

A Type II error is a [false negative](#false-negative){.no-glossary-tooltip}: failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false. The Type II error probability is the probability of missing a specified true difference. Power is the probability of detecting that difference: the true-positive probability, equal to 1 minus the Type II error probability.

For example, 90% power at a true 30-percentage-point difference means about 90 true positives and 10 false negatives per 100 repetitions of the planned trial. Here, positive means a statistically significant treatment difference, and negative means that the test did not find sufficient evidence of a difference.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-Type I error probability-meaning">
<summary>Common misconception: Type I error probability of 5% means a significant result has a 5% probability of being a false positive</summary>

If the treatments truly have equal population relief probabilities, a test with a 5% Type I error probability would give about 5 false positives per 100 repeated studies, under its assumptions. This is different from saying that 5% of all significant findings are false positives. That percentage also depends on how often real treatment differences exist and on the studies' power.

</details>

Type I error probability of 5% and power of 80% or 90% are common planning choices. Your choices should reflect the clinical question and the consequences of each error. Error probabilities describe how often each mistake occurs under specified assumptions. For the chronic pain trial, a false positive could contribute to adopting an ineffective treatment that adds adverse effects or burden. A false negative could delay recognition of a worthwhile benefit. The consequences depend on the treatment and available alternatives. These considerations should inform the planned error probabilities, alongside relevant methodological and regulatory guidance. A non-significant result may reflect insufficient information to distinguish the treatments.

## Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies {#activity-1-one-study-then-many .core-heading}

The pilot observed 70% versus 30% relief. The simulation uses assumed population percentages of 60% versus 30% to examine the chosen calculation target. The simulation now asks what studies would show if those planning values were the true population probabilities. The 60% value defines the hypothetical population explored in this simulation.

In this simulation, the population event probabilities are specified as 30% pain relief with standard treatment and 60% with the novel treatment: a true population difference of 30 percentage points. Each simulated trial samples different patients, so its observed percentages and treatment difference vary.

### A couple of individual trials {.core-heading}

Before inspecting the results, which quantities would you expect to stay fixed and which would change across three trials? With 20 patients per group and the same population assumptions, the trials could give the following results:

```{r pain-sample-estimates}
# <- saves a result under a name. lapply() repeats the same steps for each trial.
# The population probabilities stay fixed; each run generates new patients.
example_trials <- lapply(20260941:20260943, function(trial_seed) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 20,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    seed = trial_seed)
  simulate_one_study(scenario)
})
# Combine one row per trial into a table. [[i]] selects trial i from the list.
trial_examples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(example_trials), function(i) {
  trial <- example_trials[[i]]
  # For 0/1 outcomes, the mean within each group is its observed relief fraction.
  rates <- tapply(trial$data$outcome, trial$data$group, mean)
  data.frame(Trial = i, `Standard treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Control"]),
    `Novel treatment: observed relief` = percent(rates["Treatment"]),
    `Observed difference` = paste0(round(100 * trial$result$estimate), " percentage points"),
    check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}))
# kable() formats the results as a readable table.
knitr::kable(trial_examples, caption = "Three simulated trials with 20 patients per group, all sampled under the same 30% and 60% population event probabilities.")
```

The population assumptions stay the same across these trials. Their observed relief percentages, differences and testing decisions vary. In a real trial, you observe the sample and estimate the population parameters; the simulation makes that distinction visible because its population parameters are known by construction.

### Many trials and a larger sample {.core-heading}

Repeating the trial 5,000 times shows a range of possible sample differences. The larger samples generally give estimates closer to the specified population difference, although any individual trial can still differ from it.

```{r three-samples}
# c() collects the three patient counts to compare.
sample_sizes <- c(20, 50, 80)
# Repeat 5,000 trials at each count; n is patients per group, B is trials.
batches <- lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  scenario <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = n,
    p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
    width_target = .20, B = 5000, seed = 20260921 + n)
  simulate_trials(scenario)
})
# Extract and combine each batch's percentage of significant results.
power_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(batches, power_row))
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Patients per group` = power_results$n_per_group,
  `Statistically significant results` = percent(power_results$simulated_power),
  check.names = FALSE), caption = "Percentage of 5,000 simulated trials detecting the assumed 30-percentage-point population difference at each sample size.")
```

```{r sample-differences, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Observed treatment differences across 5,000 simulated trials at each sample size. The dashed line marks the specified population difference of 30 percentage points. Larger samples generally produce less variable estimates.", fig.alt="Three histograms of observed relief differences with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, showing progressively narrower distributions around the same population difference of 30 percentage points."}
local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  for (batch in batches) {
    hist(100 * batch$results$estimate, breaks = seq(-100, 100, 5),
      xlim = c(-40, 90), col = "#b9d4f3", border = "white",
      main = paste(batch$spec$n, "patients per group"),
      xlab = "Observed difference in relief (percentage points)", ylab = "Number of trials")
    abline(v = 30, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#69509a")
  }
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:sample-differences) shows [sampling variability](#sampling-variability); the table shows how often the planned test detects the specified population difference. The assumed true difference here equals the 30-point [target difference](#target-difference) used to evaluate power. The simulation uses the specified population probabilities of 30% and 60%.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

[Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) connects fixed population assumptions to changing trial results and compares what happens with larger samples.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-sample-versus-population">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Within a batch of trials, the specified population relief probabilities stay at 30% and 60%, so their true difference stays at 30 percentage points. The sample size, allocation, analysis, Type I error probability and clinical threshold also stay fixed. The patients sampled, observed relief counts and percentages, estimated difference, [p-value](#p-value) and testing decision can change from trial to trial.

A larger sample gives each trial more information, which generally reduces the sampling variability of its estimate. Increasing the sample size deliberately changes the design; it can also increase power at the same true effect. More simulation repetitions make the estimated percentage of significant results more stable. Each individual trial still has the same number of patients and the same power.

</details>

:::

This repeated-study approach follows the introductory teaching idea in @superpowerbook2022 and the use of simulation in health-sciences education [@thiesmeier2024; @rudolph2021]. The [advanced simulation explanation](#precision-of-a-simulation) examines how precisely a simulation estimates study performance.

The advanced chapter on [power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) explains the sampling-distribution diagrams and the pilot's significance boundary. The simple simulation here provides the background needed for the basic calculations.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- A sample size calculation starts with the research question and planned analysis.
- A pilot result describes its sample; relevant evidence and uncertainty inform the main study assumptions.
- Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference.
- More patients change a study's power; more simulation repetitions make its estimated performance more stable.
- The target difference and clinical threshold have distinct roles and may have the same value.

</div>

render_chapter_quiz("clinical-question")
```

# Calculating sample size {#calculations .core-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Calculate approximate sample sizes for two independent proportions or means.
- Explain how the [target difference](#target-difference), variability, [Type I error probability](#alpha) and target [power](#statistical-power) affect the calculation.
- Distinguish per-group from total counts.
- Identify the procedure, inputs and rounding behind a calculation.
:::

You can now apply these ideas to two-arm treatment comparisons. The formulas below assume two [independent groups](#independent-groups) with equal allocation and a [two-sided test](#two-sided-test). Studies that randomize hospitals, compare body sites within participants, or collect repeated measurements require calculations that account for dependence; see [units of randomization, measurement, and analysis](#units-of-analysis). [Recruitment and feasibility](#feasibility) then considers whether you can obtain enough usable outcomes; the [reporting chapter](#reporting) brings the calculation and its justification together.

Having specified the chronic pain target difference and acceptable error risks, you can calculate the required number of analyzable patients. The first calculation concerns that trial; the next concerns a continuous-outcome comparison.

## How error probabilities and power affect sample size {#how-error-rates-and-power-affect-sample-size .core-heading}

Your sample size calculation needs to account for two choices: the acceptable Type I error probability and the target power. A lower Type I error probability requires stronger evidence before concluding that the treatments differ. Higher power means a greater probability of detecting the target difference if it is the true population difference. Both generally require more patients when the other assumptions remain unchanged.

For the normal-approximation formulas below, these choices are combined into a sample size multiplier, $M$:

\begin{equation}
M=\left(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}\right)^2.
(\#eq:multiplier)
\end{equation}

Here, $\alpha$ is the Type I error probability, $\beta$ is the [Type II error probability](#beta), and $1-\beta$ is the target power. The two $z$-values translate these probabilities into positions on the standard normal distribution: the familiar bell-shaped curve, centered at zero with a standard deviation of one.

A [$z$-value](#z-value){.no-glossary-tooltip} describes how many standard deviations a position lies from the center of that curve. Its subscript gives the proportion of the distribution below that position. For example, $z_{0.975}=1.96$ means that 97.5% of the distribution lies below 1.96. This position is called a [quantile](#quantile){.no-glossary-tooltip}.

For a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%:

- The 5% error allowance is split between the two ends of the distribution: 2.5% in each tail. This gives $z_{1-0.05/2}=z_{0.975}\approx1.96$.
- The target power of 90% gives $z_{0.90}\approx1.28$.
- The multiplier is therefore approximately $(1.96+1.28)^2\approx10.51$, using the unrounded $z$-values.

This multiplier combines the chosen error probabilities and power. The sample size calculation also uses the target difference and variability. You can use the table below without calculating the $z$-values yourself. The appropriate calculation still depends on your study design and planned analysis [@kirkwood2003; @wang2020].

```{r multiplier}
# Probabilities are entered as decimals: .05 = 5%, .90 = 90%.
alpha <- .05
target_power <- .90
# qnorm() finds standard-normal cutoffs. Divide alpha by 2 for two tails.
# Add the cutoffs, then square the sum (^2) to obtain the multiplier M.
M <- (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(target_power))^2
M
```

For a Type I error probability of 5% and target power of 90%, the multiplier is $M=$ `r round(M, 2)`.

```{r multiplier-table, echo=FALSE}
grid <- expand.grid(alpha = c(.05, .01), power = c(.80, .90, .95))
grid$multiplier <- with(grid, (qnorm(1 - alpha / 2) + qnorm(power))^2)
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(grid, c("alpha", "power")), digits = 2,
  caption = "Normal-approximation sample-size multipliers for different Type I error probability and target-power choices.")
```

The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) identifies the procedures used here and explains what should accompany an exported calculation.

## Two proportions {.core-heading}

The event percentages in each group and the target difference between them are your starting inputs. For the chronic pain trial, the calculation assumes 60% relief with the novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment: a target difference of 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

For two independent groups of equal size and a two-sided test, the tutorial and apps use the normal approximation in R's `power.prop.test()` [@rcore]. You specify the two event probabilities, Type I error probability and target power. The result is the required analyzable number per group, before allowing for losses.

```{r proportions}
# Relief probabilities for novel treatment (t) and standard treatment (c).
pi_t <- .60
pi_c <- .30
# With n omitted, R finds patients per group for the requested power.
# two.sided allows either direction; strict = TRUE counts both rejection tails.
pain_plan <- power.prop.test(p1 = pi_t, p2 = pi_c,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n selects the calculated count. ceiling() rounds upward to a whole patient.
n_raw <- pain_plan$n
n_per_group <- ceiling(n_raw)
# Retain this count for the later recruitment example.
pain_lab_n <- n_per_group
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r proportions-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Analyzable sample size for the chronic pain trial using the normal planning approximation.")
```

The unrounded result is `r round(n_raw, 2)` patients per group. Rounding upward gives `r n_per_group` per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. This is the count used in the recruitment and fixed-sample sensitivity examples below. The `strict = TRUE` setting counts significant results in either direction for the two-sided test.

The calculation targets 90% power under the stated assumptions. Actual power for the planned test can differ because the calculation is approximate; simulation lets you examine that performance. Your report should identify the method, assumptions and rounding, and account for expected losses separately.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-definitive-sample">
<summary>Common misconception: the calculator provides one definitive minimum number</summary>

The calculated sample size depends on the effect, event probabilities or variability, error targets and analysis method you specify. It is a conditional planning result. You should check plausible alternative assumptions and whether the reported number is per group or for the whole study before interpreting it.

</details>

```{r proportion-changes}
# Each row specifies a different set of assumptions.
proportion_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Smaller difference", "Lower probabilities",
               "Type I error probability 1%", "Power 95%"),
  treatment = c(.60, .60, .30, .60, .60),
  control = c(.30, .45, .15, .30, .30),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
# mapply() calculates a sample size for each row using its four inputs.
proportion_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_proportions,
  proportion_cases$treatment, proportion_cases$control,
  proportion_cases$alpha, proportion_cases$power)
proportion_cases$total <- 2 * proportion_cases$per_group
# Convert probabilities to percentages for display; calculations use decimals.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(proportion_cases,
  c("treatment", "control", "alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative binary-outcome assumptions, using the same normal planning approximation as the tutorial and apps.")
```

For a yes/no outcome, the calculation uses the event percentage in each group. For example, 30% versus 15% and 60% versus 45% both differ by 15 percentage points, but they need not require the same sample size. The amount of [sampling variability](#sampling-variability) also depends on where those percentages lie. Halving the difference therefore does not necessarily multiply the required sample size by exactly four. The table lets you compare these assumptions directly.

Read a row as a conditional statement: if those event probabilities and that analysis are reasonable, then this is the approximate number required for the specified error targets. The smaller-difference row needs more participants because sampling variability makes that difference harder to distinguish from zero.

In [Activity: Two-proportion calculator](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_proportions/), you can compare the sample sizes needed at different power targets.

### Preventing gestational diabetes {#adherence .core-heading}

Suppose you want to find out whether probiotic supplementation prevents gestational diabetes in pregnant women with overweight or obesity (BMI at least 25 kg/m²). Randomly allocate women to probiotics or no probiotics, with otherwise comparable care, and assess gestational diabetes using a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). Your plan should specify the supplement, diagnostic criteria and assessment time before planning. An assessment at 20–24 weeks needs justification against applicable clinical guidance: NICE generally recommends risk-based testing at 24–28 weeks [@nicegdm]. For an observational study of supplementation, confounding requires an appropriate analysis and planning method.

For this calculation only, assume gestational diabetes occurs in 20% without probiotics and is expected in 8% with probiotics: an expected reduction of 12 percentage points. You can choose a target reduction of 10 points, corresponding to 20% versus 10%, and a [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) of 5 points. All these values are hypothetical teaching assumptions.

The same planning assumption can be expressed using either developing the disease or remaining free of it:

| Outcome entered | Without probiotics | With probiotics |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Develops gestational diabetes | 20% | 10% |
| Remains free of gestational diabetes | 80% | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:gdm-outcome-direction) Two ways to express the same assumed effect of probiotics.

The [binary-outcome calculation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=probiotics_calculation) uses the second row so that a positive treatment-minus-control difference represents benefit. A 10-percentage-point increase in remaining disease-free is the same comparison as a 10-percentage-point reduction in developing the disease. Your report should state which event you entered and its direction; the clinical question remains prevention of gestational diabetes.

```{r adherence-case}
# Load the same example inputs used by the app.
adherence_case <- teaching_case("adherence")
adherence_plan <- teaching_case_spec("adherence")
# Calculate patients per group for the example's target power.
adherence_plan$n <- plan_n(adherence_plan, "testing",
  adherence_case$inputs$target_power)
# Display the analysis count, loss-adjusted recruitment, and resulting power.
c(analyzable_per_group = adherence_plan$n,
  recruit_per_group = adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,
    adherence_case$inputs$dropout),
  planning_power = spec_power(adherence_plan))
```

```{r adherence-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=adherence_plan$n, `Recruit per group`=adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n,adherence_case$inputs$dropout), `Planning power`=percent(spec_power(adherence_plan)),check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size and recruitment requirements for the hypothetical gestational-diabetes prevention trial.")
```

[Activity: Probiotics: calculate a binary-outcome sample size](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=probiotics_calculation) explores how a smaller target difference changes the required sample and recruitment target.

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Advanced: simulate the prevention trial</summary>

The [probiotics simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=adherence) explores how the selected design performs when the true event probabilities differ from its planning assumptions.

</details>

Under these assumptions, the required recruitment total is `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(adherence_plan$n, adherence_case$inputs$dropout)`, exceeding the proposed limit of 240. This is a reason to reconsider recruitment, collaboration or the study's aim. Increasing the assumed benefit merely to obtain a smaller n would not supply the missing evidence.

## Two means {.core-heading}

For a continuous outcome, you should identify the target difference and the [standard deviation](#standard-deviation) in the same measurement units before calculating.

In the formula below, $n$ is the number of patients needed in each group, $\delta$ is the target difference between the group means, and $\sigma$ is the assumed SD of individual scores within each group. The calculation assumes the same SD in both groups. The multiplier $M$ combines the error-probability and power choices explained above:

\begin{equation}
n\approx M\frac{2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}.
(\#eq:means)
\end{equation}

Suppose an earlier study observed a 4-unit [between-group difference](#expected-difference) in a normally distributed improvement score. You can use a more conservative 3-unit target difference, with SD 5 in both groups, while patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically important. The example uses a hypothetical, approximately normally distributed improvement score. The Type I error probability is 5% and target power is 90%.

```{r means}
# Target mean difference and common standard deviation, in score units.
delta <- 3
sigma <- 5
# Insert the inputs into the normal formula, then round upward.
# The factor 2 allows for variability in both independent groups.
n_per_group <- ceiling(M * 2 * sigma^2 / delta^2)
c(per_group = n_per_group, total = 2 * n_per_group)
```

```{r means-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=n_per_group, `Analyzable total`=2*n_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate analyzable sample size for the continuous-outcome comparison.")
```

Using the multiplier of approximately 10.51, a target difference of 3 units, and an SD of 5 units:

\[
n\approx10.51\times\frac{2\times5^2}{3^2}\approx58.4.
\]

You therefore round upward to `r n_per_group` patients per group, or `r 2 * n_per_group` in total. Smaller differences are harder to distinguish from patient-to-patient variation and require larger samples.

<details>
<summary>Raw and standardized differences</summary>

The target difference of 3 score units is a raw between-group difference. Dividing it by the common SD gives the standardized difference: $d=3/5=0.60$. If the SD were 10 units, the same 3-unit difference would give $d=0.30$. The clinical difference is unchanged, but it is smaller relative to patient-to-patient variation and requires more patients to detect. A standardized effect is therefore not, by itself, a measure of clinical importance. Keeping the difference in the outcome's original units helps you explain what it would mean clinically; standardized measures can help compare results across scales [@kallogjeri2023].

</details>

<details>
<summary>Where does the assumed SD come from?</summary>

Previous studies can inform the SD, but their patients, measurement scale, follow-up time and analysis should be relevant to your study. The SD of change from baseline is not interchangeable with the SD of final scores. A review of knee osteoarthritis trials found substantial variation in pain-score variability across studies [@bentin2026]. Its estimates concern continuous WOMAC pain scores. The binary pain-relief example requires assumptions about event percentages.

Your study plan should identify the source of the assumed SD and explore a plausible range. Table \@ref(tab:mean-changes) shows what happens when the SD doubles; a published pooled SD should not be treated as a universal value for every pain study.

</details>

The simple formula helps explain how sample size depends on the target difference and variability. A calculation for the planned t test also accounts for the fact that the study must estimate variability from its patients. It therefore gives a slightly different sample size:

```{r t-test-planning}
# Plan for two independent means using the two-sample t test.
# strict = TRUE includes rejection in either direction.
t_plan <- power.t.test(delta = 3, sd = 5, sig.level = .05,
  power = .90, type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)
# Print the settings and unrounded result before rounding each group upward.
t_plan
c(per_group = ceiling(t_plan$n), total = 2 * ceiling(t_plan$n))
```

```{r t-test-planning-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Normal approximation", "Planned two-sample t test"), `Analyzable per group`=c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), `Analyzable total`=2*c(n_per_group,ceiling(t_plan$n)), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Sample size requirements under two planning methods.")
```

For your protocol, you should use the calculation that matches the planned analysis. The two methods give different counts because they use different statistical approximations. You should round upward within each group before doubling the count; recruitment losses are considered separately.

Your study plan should record the input values, software or formula, whether the test is one-sided or two-sided, allocation and rounded counts.

Established software can help with straightforward calculations when its procedure and inputs match your study. The advanced [software and statistical support guide](#software-support) reviews free and paid options and explains when early advice from a statistician is useful. Its [worked example](#gpower-assumptions) shows how an effect-size input can change the result.

<details>
<summary>Why calculation methods can give different answers</summary>

The mean calculation here assumes the same population SD in both groups and plans a pooled two-sample t test. R's default `t.test()` uses Welch's method, which allows unequal variances; choosing that analysis needs matching planning assumptions. Similarly, continuity corrections or exact methods can change binary results. Matching methods matters more than forcing two calculators to display the same number [@rcore; @julious2023].

</details>

```{r mean-changes}
# Each row changes a planning assumption from the original example.
mean_cases <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Original", "Half the difference", "Twice the SD",
               "Type I error probability 1%", "Power 95%"),
  difference = c(3, 1.5, 3, 3, 3), sd = c(5, 5, 10, 5, 5),
  alpha = c(.05, .05, .05, .01, .05),
  power = c(.90, .90, .90, .90, .95))
# Apply the normal-approximation formula to each row.
mean_cases$per_group <- mapply(sample_size_two_means,
  mean_cases$difference, mean_cases$sd, mean_cases$alpha, mean_cases$power)
mean_cases$total <- 2 * mean_cases$per_group
# Display the counts, with error probabilities and power as percentages.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(mean_cases, c("alpha", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable sample sizes under alternative mean differences, variability and error targets, using the simple normal approximation.")
```

Before rounding, halving the difference or doubling the SD multiplies the required sample size by four. You can explain this relationship using equation \@ref(eq:means).

The [Activity: Rehabilitation: calculate a mean-difference sample size](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation_calculation) lets you compare sample requirements as the target difference or SD changes.

### A rehabilitation case {#rehabilitation .core-heading}

The same calculation can compare two rehabilitation programs. Suppose the primary outcome is improvement at six weeks on a hypothetical continuous mobility score. The difference observed in previous data is 4 units, the target difference is 3 units, and patients and clinicians judge a 2-unit benefit clinically meaningful. The assumed common SD is 5 units. For this illustration, independent patients are randomized to the two programs and the improvement scores are approximately normal.

```{r rehabilitation-case}
# Load the rehabilitation example shared with the app.
rehabilitation_case <- teaching_case("rehabilitation")
rehabilitation_plan <- teaching_case_spec("rehabilitation")
# Calculate patients per group from the difference, SD, error probability and power.
rehabilitation_plan$n <- sample_size_two_means(
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_delta, rehabilitation_case$inputs$plan_sd,
  rehabilitation_case$inputs$alpha, rehabilitation_case$inputs$target_power)
# Allow for expected losses separately when calculating recruitment.
c(analyzable_per_group = rehabilitation_plan$n,
  total = 2 * rehabilitation_plan$n,
  recruitment_total = 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n,
    rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout))
```

```{r rehabilitation-case-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=rehabilitation_plan$n, `Analyzable total`=2*rehabilitation_plan$n, `Recruit total`=2*adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout), check.names=FALSE), caption="Sample size and recruitment requirements for the rehabilitation comparison.")
```

[Activity: Rehabilitation: calculate a mean-difference sample size](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation_calculation). Before changing the SD from 5 to 7, how would you expect the required sample size to change? Your exploration should hold the target difference, error probabilities and analysis fixed. Greater individual variability makes the same mean difference harder to distinguish, so the plan needs more patients. You can then assess whether 10% expected loss and a recruitment limit of 200 make each plan feasible. Although an improvement score uses before/after information within each patient, this example analyzes one score per patient across two independent groups. A single-group paired comparison, repeated-measures model, or baseline-adjusted analysis needs its own planning method.

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Advanced: simulate rehabilitation outcomes</summary>

The [rehabilitation simulation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=rehabilitation) uses a t-test planning method. *One study* generates independent, normally distributed improvement scores. Its test evaluates evidence against a zero population difference. *Many studies* shows how conclusions vary under the same population assumptions. This optional advanced extension can be used after the core calculation.

</details>

The expected-loss adjustment gives a recruitment total of `r 2 * adjust_for_dropout(rehabilitation_plan$n, rehabilitation_case$inputs$dropout)`, below this example's cap of 200. Meeting the cap and power target still leaves questions about the credibility of the assumptions, measurement quality and the clinical relevance of the target difference.

## Discharge percentages {#discharge .core-heading}

In this optional practice, you compare three sample size plans for the same hospital-discharge trial. The aim is to see how a relative increase differs from an increase in percentage points, and how the target difference and target power affect the number of patients needed.

Suppose a hospital is planning a trial of a new discharge-support program against standard care. The outcome is discharge within seven days of admission: yes or no. With standard care, 80% of patients are expected to be discharged by then. All values in this example are hypothetical.

For the new program, the [difference observed in earlier data](#expected-difference) is 18 percentage points (98% versus 80%), and the clinical threshold is 8 percentage points. These remain fixed reference values. Each plan below specifies the target difference used in its calculation. All three plans use equal group sizes, a two-sided test, a 5% Type I error probability, and no allowance for losses at this stage.

| Plan | Target difference | Target power |
|:--|:--|:--|
| A | A 20% relative increase from the 80% standard-care percentage | 80% |
| B | An absolute increase of 10 [percentage points](#percentage-points) | 80% |
| C | The same target difference as Plan A | 90% |

Table: (\#tab:discharge-task) Three discharge-study plans with a 5% Type I error probability and a two-sided comparison.

### Your task {.unnumbered}

The short note below contains proposed interpretations of the three plans. Reviewing it gives you a prediction to check with the calculator.

```{r discharge-error-review, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("discharge")
```

1. You can calculate each plan using the [two-proportions method](#two-proportions) or [Activity: Discharge percentages](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge). In the app's *Settings*, the standard-treatment percentage stays at 80%; the novel-treatment percentage and target power should match the plan. The *Overview* shows the required sample size. Your record should include both the analyzable count per group and the total. Each per-group count is rounded upward before doubling for two equal groups.
2. Your explanation should connect the results to the target difference and power chosen in each plan. Which parts of the proposed interpretation would you retain, and which would you revise?

<details>
<summary>Show the calculation and interpretation</summary>

```{r discharge-answers}
# A relative increase multiplies 80% by 1.20; an absolute increase adds .10.
discharge <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("20% relative increase", "10 percentage points", "Higher power"),
  control = .80, treatment = c(.80 * 1.20, .80 + .10, .80 * 1.20),
  power = c(.80, .80, .90))
# Recalculate for each treatment probability and power target.
discharge$per_group <- mapply(function(p, power) {
  sample_size_two_proportions(p, .80, alpha = .05, power = power)
}, discharge$treatment, discharge$power)
discharge$total <- 2 * discharge$per_group
# Show per-group and total counts with probabilities formatted as percentages.
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(discharge, c("control", "treatment", "power")),
  caption = "Analyzable discharge-study sample sizes using the normal planning approximation in power.prop.test().")
```

The treatment percentages are 96%, 90% and 96%, giving target differences of 16, 10 and 16 percentage points for A, B and C. The approximate totals are `r paste(discharge$total, collapse = ", ")`, respectively. Plan B needs more patients than A because its smaller target difference is harder to detect at the same power. Plan C needs more patients than A because it aims for higher power at the same difference. Of these three plans, B requires the most patients. The difference observed in previous data remains 18 points and the clinical threshold remains 8 points in each comparison.

Figure \@ref(fig:discharge-grids) shows how the relative increase in Plans A and C and the absolute increase in Plan B translate into discharge percentages.

```{r discharge-grids, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap="Discharge percentages in illustrative groups of 100 patients. A 20% relative increase from 80% gives 96%; an increase of 10 percentage points gives 90%. The grids display assumed percentages; the sample size calculation determines how many patients the study requires.", fig.alt="Three grids of 100 squares. Standard care has 80 discharged and 20 not discharged. A 20% relative increase adds 16 discharges, giving 96 of 100. An increase of 10 percentage points adds 10 discharges, giving 90 of 100."}
draw_discharge_grids()
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-percentage-points">
<summary>Common misconception: percentages and percentage points are interchangeable</summary>

From a baseline of 80%, a 20% relative increase gives 96% ($0.80\times1.20=0.96$), an increase of 16 percentage points. An increase of 20 percentage points gives 100%. The baseline and whether the change is relative or absolute should be clear before you enter probabilities into a calculator.

</details>

</details>

The advanced [discharge simulation](#discharge-simulation) examines how the approximation performs when the assumed event probability is close to 100%.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Two-group calculations depend on the target difference, variability or event probabilities, Type I error probability and power.
- The result should identify analyzable participants per group and in total.
- Expected losses are allowed for separately when determining recruitment.
- The [reporting chapter](#reporting) brings the method, inputs, software and rounding together.

</div>
