# Recruitment and feasibility {#feasibility .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Adjust an analyzable sample size for expected losses and round within each group.
- Explain why missing outcomes also require prevention and an appropriate analysis.
- Explain how treatment changes can affect the difference between randomized groups and the recruitment plan.
- Assess one plausible alternative assumption and the practical recruitment requirement.

:::

The chronic pain calculation in [Chapter 2](#two-proportions) requires `r pain_lab_n` patients in each group with a usable four-week outcome. The clinics now need a recruitment target. Some patients may miss that assessment; others may change treatment and still provide their outcome. These possibilities affect different parts of the plan.

You first allow for expected missing outcomes, then consider how treatment changes could affect the between-group difference. Finally, you check whether the clinics can recruit enough patients and whether the plan remains workable under less favorable assumptions. The [reporting chapter](#reporting) brings the resulting decisions together.

## Account for expected losses {.core-heading}



If some recruited patients are expected to have no usable outcome, you will need to recruit more patients than the calculation requires for analysis. Here, $n$ is the required number per group and $r$ is the expected proportion lost, so $1-r$ is the expected [retention proportion](#retention). The brackets mean "round upward to the next whole patient":

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{recruit,arm}}=\left\lceil\frac{n}{1-r}\right\rceil.
(\#eq:dropout)
\end{equation}

The expected loss should draw on studies or records with a comparable population, treatment, outcome and follow-up period. For example, if 20 of 200 enrolled patients in a comparable study lacked the required outcome, the observed loss was 20/200 = 10%. Using $r=0.10$ in a new study assumes that this experience is relevant. Reasons for missing outcomes, differences between arms and uncertainty in a small pilot should inform that judgment. When evidence is limited, your report should identify a plausible range and show how recruitment changes across it; there is no universal default loss percentage.

```{r recruitment}
# Start with the 56 patients per group needed for analysis.
analyzable_per_group <- pain_lab_n
# Divide by the expected retained fraction, 95%, then round upward.
recruit_per_group <- ceiling(analyzable_per_group / (1 - .05))
c(analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  recruit_per_group = recruit_per_group, recruit_total = 2 * recruit_per_group)
```

```{r recruitment-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=analyzable_per_group, `Recruit per group`=recruit_per_group, `Recruit total`=2*recruit_per_group, check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Chronic-pain recruitment target allowing for 5% expected loss.")
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout-arithmetic">
<summary>Common misconception: allowing for 10% dropout means adding 10%</summary>

If you expect 10% of participants to be lost, approximately 90% will remain. You should therefore divide the required analyzable sample size by 0.90. For example, 100 analyzable participants require recruiting 112 participants after rounding up. This allows for the expected loss; the actual number retained may differ.

</details>

For the chronic pain trial, 5% expected loss means approximately 95% of recruits will contribute to the analysis. To obtain `r analyzable_per_group` patients per group with usable outcomes, you would plan to recruit `r analyzable_per_group`/0.95 = `r round(analyzable_per_group / .95, 2)`, rounded upward to `r recruit_per_group` per group.

<span id="model-answer-protocol-counts"></span>
The protocol should report both the required [analyzable sample](#analyzable-sample-size) and the recruitment target, per group and in total: here, `r 2 * analyzable_per_group` analyzable patients and `r 2 * recruit_per_group` recruits across the two groups. Actual retention can vary.

The percentage of participants lost to follow-up may differ between treatment groups. This is called *differential dropout*. For example, outcomes might be missing for 20% of participants receiving the novel treatment and 10% receiving standard treatment. When such differences are anticipated, sample size planning should account for the expected retention in each group and the planned allocation ratio. A single overall dropout percentage can conceal a shortfall in one group.

The reasons for missing outcomes also matter. In the chronic pain trial, patients who experience little relief might be more likely to miss the final assessment. If this happens more often in the novel-treatment group, an analysis restricted to participants with observed outcomes could overestimate its benefit. [Bias](#bias) can occur with equal or unequal dropout percentages. Assessing it requires information about why outcomes are missing, the treatment effect being estimated, and the analysis used [@bell2013dropout].

Your study plan should describe how missing outcomes will be minimized, how their reasons will be recorded in each group, and how the analysis will handle them. [Sensitivity analyses](#sensitivity-analysis) should examine whether conclusions change under plausible alternative assumptions about the missing outcomes [@little2012missing].

The usual simulations start with the stated number of patients available for analysis. The advanced [missing-outcome extension](#explore-missing-outcomes) starts with recruited participants and explores equal, unequal, and outcome-related losses in the [repeated-trial activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation).

The [Activity: Adjust recruitment](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=recruitment) explores how shared or different expected losses change the recruitment target.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-dropout">
<summary>Common misconception: recruiting extra participants resolves missing-data problems</summary>

Recruiting extra participants can help preserve the analyzable sample size and statistical power. Addressing missing-data bias requires prevention, appropriate analysis, and sensitivity analyses alongside the recruitment allowance [@little2012missing].

</details>

## Treatment changes and other anticipated events {#treatment-changes .core-heading}

Participants may stop their assigned treatment, miss doses, switch to the other treatment, or receive additional treatment during follow-up. These changes can affect the difference between randomized groups and the sample size needed for the planned power. For example, patients assigned to standard treatment might start the novel treatment, making the groups' outcomes more similar. This is a form of [treatment contamination](#treatment-contamination) [@wittes2002].

Treatment discontinuation and loss to follow-up should be recorded separately. When your question concerns the effect of assignment to treatment, participants are analyzed in their randomized groups and follow-up continues wherever possible. This treatment-policy approach follows the [estimand framework](#estimand); the protocol and SAP specify follow-up and missing-data methods [@iche9r1]. Excluding patients because they switched treatments can introduce bias [@dodd2017].

Your sample size assumptions should reflect the treatment changes expected in your study and the treatment effect you intend to estimate. If the outcome percentages or mean difference already incorporate realistic adherence, an additional adjustment for the same changes would count their impact twice [@iche9r1]. Table \@ref(tab:anticipated-events) summarizes the implications of common events.

| Anticipated event | Implication for planning |
|:--|:--|
| Missing final assessments, unusable samples, or equipment failure | Allow for the expected percentage of unavailable primary outcomes, considering each group separately. |
| Treatment switching or contamination | Account for the resulting difference between randomized groups when calculating sample size. |
| Missed doses, early treatment discontinuation, or rescue medication | Consider how the timing and extent of these changes affect outcomes and the treatment effect being estimated. |
| Death before a planned assessment | Specify how death enters the research question and outcome definition. A pain score after death is undefined; the study design and analysis need an explicit approach. |

Table: (\#tab:anticipated-events) Anticipated events and their implications for sample size planning. Treatment changes and events such as death require an approach matched to the research question [@iche9r1].

Does switching treatment mean that a patient is lost from the study? Figure \@ref(fig:treatment-followup) helps separate two aspects of follow-up that affect planning: which treatment a patient receives, and whether the four-week outcome is available. You can follow each shaded row from randomized group, through treatment received, to final assessment.

```{r treatment-followup, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.3, fig.cap="Following the chronic pain trial after randomization. Each row retains the original assigned group. The middle column shows treatment received; the final column shows whether pain relief at four weeks was recorded. Switching can change the treatment difference, while missing outcomes reduce the observed-outcome count. Both matter for sample size planning.", fig.alt="Three numbered columns show randomized group, treatment received, and four-week outcome. Each of the novel and standard randomized groups branches into receiving the assigned treatment or switching. Either treatment path can have an outcome recorded or missing. A participant who switches and provides an outcome remains in the originally randomized group for the effect of treatment assignment."}
draw_treatment_followup()
```

For example, a patient assigned to the novel treatment may switch to standard treatment and still report pain relief at four weeks. That recorded outcome remains in the novel-treatment group when estimating the effect of treatment assignment. The missing-outcome allowance concerns the final column; the assumed treatment difference should also reflect relevant changes in treatment received in the middle column.

```{r recruitment-error-review, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("recruitment")
```

<details class="advanced-explanation" id="treatment-switching">
<summary>Allowing for treatment switching</summary>

[Treatment crossover](#treatment-crossover){.no-glossary-tooltip} here means receiving the other treatment after randomization. A planned crossover trial, in which participants receive treatments in a prespecified sequence, requires a calculation suited to that design.

A simplified model describes complete switching between treatments. Let $a$ be the fraction assigned to the novel treatment who receive standard treatment, and $b$ the fraction assigned to standard treatment who receive the novel treatment. If switchers have the same outcome distribution as other recipients of the treatment they receive, the between-group difference becomes $1-a-b$ times the difference under full adherence. Assuming little change in outcome variance, the approximate per-group requirement is [@wittes2002]:

\begin{equation}
n_{\mathrm{switching}} \approx \frac{n_{\mathrm{full\ adherence}}}{(1-a-b)^2}.
(\#eq:switching)
\end{equation}

With 10% switching from novel to standard and 5% in the other direction, the multiplier is $1/(1-0.10-0.05)^2=1.38$: approximately 38% more participants. The squared denominator reflects the inverse-square relationship between the difference and required sample size. This approximation requires $a+b<1$.

Partial adherence, delayed switching, and switching prompted by poor response need more detailed assumptions. Methods that account for changes in variance and differences between adherence groups are available [@shardell2009].

For binary outcomes, you can recalculate sample size using the revised event percentages. As a separate sensitivity scenario for chronic pain, suppose 60% and 30% describe relief under full adherence. With the switching percentages above, the simplified model gives:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Assigned novel treatment: }&0.90(60\%)+0.10(30\%)=57\%,\\
\text{Assigned standard treatment: }&0.95(30\%)+0.05(60\%)=31.5\%.
\end{aligned}
\]

The resulting between-group difference is 25.5 percentage points. The [two-proportion app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/two_proportions/) can calculate the sample needed at these revised percentages. This sensitivity scenario changes the assumed comparison; the main example's difference observed in the pilot of 40 percentage points, target difference of 30 percentage points and clinical threshold of 20 percentage points retain their stated roles.

In the [recruitment adjustment activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=recruitment), the optional switching calculation starts with a sample size that assumes full adherence. A separate loss allowance then reflects expected outcome completeness. Intermediate values remain unrounded until the final recruitment count. For example, starting with 100 per group, the switching assumptions above and 5% missing outcomes in both groups gives $\lceil100/(0.85^2\times0.95)\rceil=146$ recruits per group. With unequal losses, equal recruitment uses the larger requirement for both groups.

Your report should document the switching assumptions, their evidence, the method used, and sensitivity to alternative assumptions. The downloadable app report includes these calculation steps and your written justification; the [reproducibility chapter](#tutorial-methods) explains the procedures.

</details>

The [recruitment adjustment activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=recruitment) includes a prediction-and-justification question with a model answer. Its advanced option explores how switching and missing assessments affect the same recruitment plan. It calculates expected requirements without generating individual patient outcomes.

## Sensitivity to planning assumptions {#stress-test-the-study-plan .core-heading}

A [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis){.no-glossary-tooltip} examines what happens when a planning assumption changes within a plausible range. For the chronic pain trial, suppose standard-treatment relief remains 30%, but the novel-treatment probability is 50% rather than the planned 60%. The difference is then 20 percentage points rather than 30. Detecting the smaller difference with the same 90% power requires more patients.

```{r pain-core-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Assumed novel-treatment relief` = c("60%", "50%"),
  `Difference from 30% standard-treatment relief` = c("30 percentage points", "20 percentage points"),
  `Analyzable patients per group for 90% power` = c(pain_lab_n,
    ceiling(power.prop.test(p1=.50, p2=.30, sig.level=.05, power=.90,
      alternative="two.sided", strict=TRUE)$n)), check.names=FALSE),
  caption="Required sample sizes under two plausible treatment differences, with other planning assumptions unchanged.")
```

The smaller difference should have a scientific justification. These comparisons belong in the planning record and can be reported in the protocol or a supplement. For example, @wang2024bep state their principal calculation in the protocol and present detectable risk ratios under alternative assumptions about outcome frequency and power in an additional file. DELTA² and CONSORT recommend documenting sensitivity to calculation inputs [@cook2018delta2; @consortee2025]. The concise [report example](#sample-size-calculation-report) states the selected calculation; this section retains the supporting alternatives. The advanced chapter on [power and uncertain assumptions](#curves) also evaluates how the original fixed sample would perform if reality differed from the plan.

<details class="misconception" id="lasagnas-law">
<summary>Common misconception: having many patients in the clinic guarantees enough recruits</summary>

*Lasagna's law* describes the tendency to overestimate how many patients will actually be available for a study. Eligibility criteria, willingness to participate, competing studies, and practical barriers can substantially reduce recruitment [@lasagna1979].

In a prospective survey, investigators' average forecast for reaching recruitment targets was 78.8%, compared with 42.7% actually succeeding among 281 evaluated trials. For completing primary data collection on time, the corresponding figures were 72.2% and 13.4% among 536 trials [@benjamin2022forecasts]. The [advanced discussion](#planning-uncertainty) explains the survey's limitations. These findings support allowing for uncertainty in recruitment and timing.

For the chronic pain trial, recruitment estimates should draw on recent screening and enrollment records. For example, if 100 potentially relevant patients are seen each month, 40 meet the eligibility criteria, and half of those consent, expected recruitment is 20 participants per month. Your plan should also consider slower recruitment and delays in opening study sites.

</details>

## Options when the study provides insufficient information {#what-if-the-study-is-too-small-for-its-purpose .core-heading}

### Underpowered studies {#underpowered-studies .core-heading}



A study with low power often misses the specified true difference. A small study also produces more variable estimates. When its power is low, the studies that achieve statistical significance are often those in which sampling variability makes the observed difference unusually large. If you look only at significant findings, you can therefore get an exaggerated impression of the treatment benefit.

Larger samples reduce [sampling variability](#sampling-variability). Addressing bias requires attention to the design, measurement and analysis.

For the chronic pain trial, 90% power at a 30-percentage-point difference means that, if relief were truly 60% versus 30%, about 90% of repetitions would reject the hypothesis of no between-group difference. With the same sample size, a smaller true difference of 20 points would be detected less often: approximate power would be `r round(100 * report_example$facts$sensitivity_power)`%.

The eventual result also needs clinical interpretation. The [estimation chapter](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) explains how an estimated difference and its uncertainty inform that assessment.

### Ways to increase power {#increase-power .core-heading}



Before collecting data, you can consider whether the design could provide more information about the treatment effect. Table \@ref(tab:increase-power) separates changes to the study from changes to its error targets.

For continuous outcomes, allocation, baseline information and within-person comparisons can affect efficiency [@candel2023]. These formulas concern continuous outcomes; binary outcomes require methods suited to event probabilities. Your protocol should prespecify useful baseline adjustment and recalculate for the intended model. A crossover design is only appropriate when treatment reversibility, disease stability and carryover permit it.

| Option | Why it can help | What to consider |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Increase the analyzable sample | More independent patients reduce sampling uncertainty at the same true effect. | For the chronic pain trial, another recruiting clinic or a longer recruitment period could supply more patients. Your plan should allow for expected losses and assess feasibility. |
| Improve follow-up and outcome completeness | Retaining more outcomes protects the analyzable sample. | For the chronic pain trial, accessible follow-up appointments and reminders may improve outcome collection. Reasons for missing outcomes still inform the analysis. |
| Improve measurement | More reliable measurement can reduce unexplained variability in a continuous outcome and improve precision. | For pain relief, a clear, consistent definition and assessment time are important. A different outcome needs its own assumptions and calculation. |
| Use an appropriate, efficient design and analysis | Prespecified adjustment for informative baseline measures, or a suitable paired or repeated-measures design, can improve precision. | For a continuous pain score, prespecified adjustment for baseline pain may improve precision. A paired design requires a suitable clinical setting. Planning must match the adjusted model or dependent observations. |
| Keep allocation balanced when appropriate | For comparisons assuming equal variances, equal group sizes make efficient use of a fixed total sample size. | The chronic pain trial assigns equal numbers to novel and standard treatment. Unequal variances or other design requirements may justify another allocation and calculation. |
| Accept a higher Type I error probability | A less stringent rejection rule increases power at the specified alternative. | It also increases the probability of rejecting a true null. The error probability should be justified prospectively; changing it to make a result significant is not sound planning. |
| Use a one-sided test when the scientific question warrants it | Directing the rejection region to a prespecified direction can increase power for effects in that direction. | It does not test both directions in the same way. Your protocol should specify and justify it before you see the data; a smaller required sample is not sufficient justification [@moye2002]. |

Table: (\#tab:increase-power) Options for increasing power and the assumptions or tradeoffs they require.

Power calculations describe performance under assumed treatment benefits. Those assumptions should be grounded in relevant evidence. Running more simulations improves the precision of the estimated power.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

You can compare plans in [Activity: Chronic pain: one study and many studies](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). You should keep standard-treatment relief at 30%, novel-treatment relief at 60% and the Type I error probability at 5%. You can compare 50 and 80 analyzable patients per group. Which plan detects the specified benefit more often?

What would obtaining the larger sample require in practice?

Your study plan should explain the recruitment implications.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-larger-study-resources">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With the same population assumptions and test, 80 analyzable patients per group should detect the 30-point difference more often than 50 per group. In the prepared simulation, estimated power is `r percent(power_results$simulated_power[3])` and `r percent(power_results$simulated_power[2])`, respectively. At 10% expected loss, the corresponding recruitment targets are 89 per group (178 total) and 56 per group (112 total), after rounding within each arm. The larger design therefore needs capacity for 66 additional recruits, with implications for recruitment time, staffing, funding and participant burden. More information can reduce uncertainty, but the feasibility of obtaining it also needs justification.

</details>

:::

If the study remains infeasible, you may need to reconsider its aim, collaborate, or decide not to proceed with an efficacy study. For example, a small preliminary pain study could estimate whether patients complete the four-week assessment. Its sample size would then follow that feasibility objective; the original treatment comparison would retain its limited power. The [pilot example](#pilot-feasibility) shows how to justify this revised purpose [@lakens2022].

Broader eligibility may make the study more representative of the intended population. If it also increases outcome variability, power at a fixed sample and treatment difference may fall. The calculation should reflect the resulting population and analysis.

Clustered designs, nonparametric analyses and Bayesian planning need methods suited to their assumptions; [Study designs and testing strategies](#study-designs) provides starting points [@hayes1999; @happ2019; @pezeshk2003]. The advanced [rare-disease section](#rare-diseases) considers a particularly restrictive recruitment ceiling.



<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- The recruitment target allows for expected unavailable outcomes, with rounding within each group.
- The reasons for missing outcomes and treatment changes affect the assumptions and analysis.
- Sensitivity analysis shows whether plausible alternatives change the recommendation.
- Recruitment estimates should use relevant screening and enrollment information.

</div>

# The sample size calculation report {#reporting .core-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .core-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Write a concise sample size calculation report supported by a study plan.
- Explain the evidence and judgments behind the numerical assumptions.
- Record the procedure, software, inputs, rounding and recruitment adjustment reproducibly.
- Recognize incomplete or inconsistent reporting and revise it.
:::

A useful report lets another researcher understand your decisions and reproduce the calculation. The concise calculation report presents the selected design and numerical result; the supporting study plan retains evidence, alternative assumptions and unresolved decisions. The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) creates both from one set of answers.

## What belongs in the report? {#record-assumptions .core-heading}

Table \@ref(tab:planning-assumptions) organizes reporting decisions under the [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question)'s four headings and links to the chapters explaining each part. Decisions needing more evidence can remain provisional. The [estimation reporting guidance](#estimation-report) gives the corresponding entries for a precision-based plan.

::: {.planning-assumptions}

| Decision | What to make explicit |
|---|---|
| **Question and design** | [Chapter 1: Research question and power](#clinical-question) introduces this section. |
| Research question: PICO | Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome, including the measurement time point |
| Intervention and comparator | What each group receives, how it is delivered, by whom and on what schedule; relevant dose or intensity and permitted additional care |
| Design, sampling and allocation | Study design, participant selection, unit of allocation and allocation ratio; any paired, repeated or clustered observations |
| **Assumptions and evidence** | [Chapter 1](#clinical-question) develops the assumptions; [Chapter 3: Recruitment and feasibility](#feasibility) examines alternatives. |
| Effect scale | Treatment minus control; score units or percentage points; direction of benefit |
| Difference observed in previous data | Observed result, source, relevance and uncertainty; gaps in the available evidence |
| Clinical threshold | Smallest worthwhile between-group benefit, justified against treatment harms, burden and alternatives |
| Target difference | Difference used in the power calculation, with justification |
| Variation or event probabilities | Common standard deviation or both groups' event percentages; source, population, outcome definition and assessment time |
| Evidence relevance and uncertainty | Whether differences in patients, care or measurement limit applicability; uncertain inputs and evidence needed |
| Sensitivity analysis | Plausible alternatives supported by the evidence review; whether sample size changes or stays fixed, and implications for the recommendation |
| **Calculation** | [Chapter 1: Research question and power](#power) explains the criteria; [Chapter 2: Calculating sample size](#calculations) supplies the calculations. |
| Planned analysis | Planned test and sidedness; how pairing or clustering will be handled, where relevant |
| Calculation procedure and software | Method or formula; software, package and code versions; saved inputs and calculation steps. For simulations: data-generating assumptions, repetitions and random-number settings. See [Methods and software to record](#reproducibility-record) |
| Type I error probability and target power | Chosen probabilities and the target difference at which power is evaluated |
| Sample size needed or available for analysis | Per-group and total analyzable counts; calculation result and upward rounding, or the available sample for an existing-data study |
| **Recruitment and conclusion** | [Chapter 3: Recruitment and feasibility](#feasibility) connects the analyzable count to a recruitment target and final justification. |
| Losses, missing data and recruitment | Expected losses, recruitment target and how missing outcomes or treatment changes affect the plan |
| Feasibility and resources | Expected recruitment rate, recruitment period, available resources and other practical constraints |
| Intended conclusion | What the design could establish and what remains uncertain |

Table: (\#tab:planning-assumptions) Decisions and assumptions to record in the study-plan activity, with links to the core chapters that develop each part of the study plan.

:::

The prompts draw on PICO, SPIRIT 2025, CONSORT 2025, [DELTA²](#delta2), and section 4.1 of the UMCG statistical analysis plan (SAP) template [@richardson1995; @spiritconsort2025; @consortee2025; @cook2018delta2; @umcgsap]. The sections below show how to describe the statistical criteria, calculation, software and recruitment decision in one report.

For each numerical assumption, your supporting plan should record its source, why that evidence applies to your study, and a plausible range. For example, the chronic pain trial needs evidence about four-week relief in patients with similar pain severity and background care. A percentage from a different population or a later assessment may be unsuitable. [Chapter 2](#two-proportions) shows why both groups' event percentages affect the required sample, even when their difference stays the same.

A concise report can retain this reasoning: why the control percentage is relevant, how uncertainty informed the target difference, and which treatment burdens justify the clinical threshold. @wang2024bep illustrate how sources support inputs, using local data for the control percentage and a systematic review for the target risk ratio. The chronic pain report in [Example 4.1](#sample-size-calculation-report) shows how the decisions developed here fit into a complete sample size calculation report.

Clear reporting also makes measurement choices open to scrutiny. In a review of 185 studies using the BREAST-Q Reconstruction Module, a patient-reported questionnaire for breast reconstruction, only 17 reported a sample-size calculation and 71 reported the primary outcome's assessment time; 36 had questionnaire-administration errors [@gallo2022]. These findings underline why your plan should specify how and when the outcome is measured alongside the calculation. Missing calculation details leave the sample-size justification unassessable.

<details class="misconception" id="model-answer-pilot-threshold">
<summary>Common misconception: the clinical threshold should follow the pilot result</summary>

If the pilot had shown relief in 6 rather than 7 treated patients, should the clinical threshold change?

The observed difference would fall from 40 to 30 percentage points, with standard-treatment relief still at 30%. That changes the evidence about the likely benefit. The clinical threshold remains 20 points because the judgment about worthwhile relief, harms and burden has not changed.

</details>

As your plan develops, brief notes about revised assumptions and their reasons will help you explain the final recommendation. The advanced [evidence and uncertainty discussion](#planning-uncertainty) shows how to examine assumptions that remain uncertain.

## Statistical criteria and their justification {#report-statistical-criteria .core-heading}

Your report should specify the Type I error probability, sidedness and target power, together with the difference at which power is evaluated. The chronic pain plan uses a two-sided test because differences in either direction matter. A Type I error probability of 5% sets the planned false-positive probability; 90% power limits the false-negative probability to 10% when the true difference is 30 percentage points under the calculation's assumptions.

The [report example](#sample-size-calculation-report) states these criteria alongside the 30-point target difference. The 20-point clinical threshold records the minimum benefit judged worthwhile. It is a separate clinical criterion; 90% power at 30 points does not imply 90% power at 20 points.

In the [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=power), you can record the error probability and power, explain their choice, and describe what the study is intended to establish.

## Calculation method, result and software {#report-calculation-method .core-heading}

A reproducible calculation identifies the procedure, its inputs, the unrounded result and how it was rounded. For the chronic pain trial, the method is a normal approximation for a two-sided pooled score test of independent proportions without continuity correction. The comparison uses equal allocation and no covariate adjustment. The report should name this procedure and the software that implements the calculation.

The [completed report](#sample-size-calculation-report) records 30% standard-treatment relief, 60% novel-treatment relief, a two-sided Type I error probability of 5% and 90% power. The calculated `r sprintf("%.2f", report_example$facts$raw_n)` patients per group are rounded upward to `r report_example$facts$analyzable`, or `r 2 * report_example$facts$analyzable` analyzable patients in total. The recruitment adjustment is explained in [Chapter 3](#feasibility).

<details class="report-methods" id="sample-size-report-methods">
<summary>Calculation procedure and software record</summary>

This calculation uses R `r report_example$r_version` and stats `r report_example$stats_version`. `stats::` identifies the package supplying `power.prop.test()`. Setting `strict = TRUE` includes rejection in either direction of the two-sided test. The [methods record](#tutorial-methods) explains the analysis and confidence interval used in the simulation app.

```{r report-command}
# Calculate patients per group for the specified event probabilities and power.
plan <- stats::power.prop.test(
  p1 = 0.60, p2 = 0.30, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.90,
  alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# $n extracts the calculated count; ceiling() rounds it upward to a whole patient.
analyzable_per_group <- ceiling(plan$n)
# c() collects the named results to display together.
c(unrounded_per_group = plan$n,
  analyzable_per_group = analyzable_per_group,
  analyzable_total = 2 * analyzable_per_group)
```

The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) includes the prepared calculation's software record when the chronic pain comparison is selected. An attached calculator result retains the inputs and software used for that result. The [reproducibility chapter](#reproducibility-record) explains the full record.

</details>

In the calculator app's Report view, “Add this calculation to my study plan” lets you review the result before attaching it. Your [calculation section](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) should explain why the method suits your design and retain its settings and versions.

## A complete sample size calculation report {#write-a-sample-size-justification .core-heading}

Your study plan holds the question, evidence, assumptions, calculations, feasibility assessment and unresolved decisions. Its sample size calculation report presents the relevant design, justified inputs, procedure, software and participant counts concisely. The activity assembles this report first, followed by the supporting study plan, from the same answers. The recruitment justification completes the report, and a final review checks that all parts agree. [Example 4.1](#sample-size-calculation-report) brings these elements together for the chronic pain trial. Its pilot results and judgments about treatment burden and follow-up provide the assumptions for this worked example; in your own report, each input should be traceable to evidence or an explicitly justified judgment.

The example follows reporting elements in SPIRIT 2025, CONSORT 2025, DELTA² and the UMCG SAP template (version 3, section 4.1) [@spiritconsort2025; @consortee2025; @cook2018delta2; @umcgsap; @roa2024comet]. The sample size calculation report, protocol and SAP should use consistent outcomes, assumptions and analysis methods.

<div class="annotated-report" role="group" aria-labelledby="sample-size-report-caption">
<p class="caption" id="sample-size-report-caption"><span id="sample-size-calculation-report">Example 4.1: Sample size calculation report for the chronic pain trial.</span></p>

<p class="report-part">Question and design</p>

The trial will <span class="report-mark">[A] individually randomize adults with chronic pain to novel or standard treatment in a 1:1 ratio. The primary outcome is patient-reported pain relief at four weeks, recorded as yes or no</span> using the same prespecified question in both groups. The treatment effect is the absolute difference in relief percentages, novel minus standard treatment.

<p class="report-part">Assumptions and evidence</p>

The pilot observed relief in 7 of 10 patients receiving novel treatment and 3 of 10 receiving standard treatment. Given the uncertainty of these small-sample estimates, the calculation uses <span class="report-mark">[B] 60% relief with novel treatment and 30% with standard treatment, a target difference of 30 percentage points</span>, below the pilot's 40-point difference. Patient and clinical advisers set the minimum worthwhile increase at 20 percentage points: one additional patient reporting relief per five treated with the novel treatment instead of standard treatment. They judged this additional relief necessary to justify four extra clinic visits and the risk of short-lived dizziness. Both groups may continue the same background pain medication.

<p class="report-part">Calculation</p>

The primary comparison will use a <span class="report-mark">[C] two-sided pooled score test for independent proportions without continuity correction or covariate adjustment</span>. A normal planning approximation with <span class="report-mark">[D] a Type I error probability of 5% and 90% power at the 30-point target difference</span> gives <span class="report-mark">[E] `r sprintf("%.2f", report_example$facts$raw_n)` analyzable patients per group, rounded upward to `r report_example$facts$analyzable` per group (`r 2 * report_example$facts$analyzable` total)</span>. The conventional two-sided 5% significance level is used; the 90% power target limits the probability of failing to detect the target difference to 10%. The calculation uses <span class="report-mark">[F] R `r report_example$r_version`, stats `r report_example$stats_version`, and `stats::power.prop.test()` with `alternative = "two.sided"` and `strict = TRUE`</span>.

<p class="report-part">Recruitment</p>

Given the short four-week assessment period, the calculation allows for <span class="report-mark">[E] 5% unavailable primary outcomes in each group. Dividing the analyzable requirement by 0.95 gives `r report_example$facts$recruitment` recruits per group: `r report_example$facts$analyzable`/0.95, rounded upward, or `r 2 * report_example$facts$recruitment` participants in total</span>.

</div>

| Label | What this part makes explicit |
|:--|:--|
| A: Question and design | Population, primary outcome, time point and allocation. |
| B: Numerical assumptions | Both event percentages, the target difference and the reasoning behind the selected values. |
| C: Procedure | The planned test, sidedness, corrections and covariate adjustment. |
| D: Statistical performance | Type I error probability and power at the specified difference. |
| E: Participant counts | Unrounded and rounded requirements, per-group and total counts, and the loss allowance. |
| F: Software | Function, settings and versions needed to repeat the calculation. |

Table: (\#tab:report-annotations) Essential elements of the sample size calculation report in Example 4.1. Letters connect the explanation to the blue annotations.

The [commented calculation](#sample-size-report-methods) reproduces the analyzable count. The [recruitment calculation](#account-for-expected-losses) shows the loss adjustment. A plan with multiple outcomes, interim analyses or sample-size adaptations also needs the [advanced design-specific record](#complex-design-record).

The report below contains several problems. Its linked explanations show how you could revise it using the decisions introduced in the core chapters.

```{r report-error-review, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_error_activity("report")
```

The [teaching guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/TEACHING_GUIDE.html#extended-sample-size-justification) provides a longer assignment and peer-review prompts. Before completing the report, you should be able to explain the evidence for the event percentages, why the selected target matters clinically, the choice of power, and the basis for the loss allowance.

Your final review should check that the percentages, target difference, power, method and counts agree across the report and attached calculations. The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=recruitment) brings together your recruitment justification and final recommendation.

## Reproducibility and supporting records {#reproducibility-record .core-heading}

The study protocol sets out the design and objectives; the statistical analysis plan (SAP) specifies the analyses in enough detail to implement them. Their outcome definitions, sample size assumptions and primary analysis should agree, with amendments documented. UMCG students and researchers can access the [UMCG statistical analysis plan template in Zenya](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78) [@umcgsap]. The [annotated report](#write-a-sample-size-justification) uses its sample-size reporting elements.

Table \@ref(tab:planning-assumptions) covers the core reporting items. The selected calculation should retain its exact inputs, software versions and rounding; the supporting record should make revised assumptions and their reasons traceable.

A simulation report should also describe how data were generated, the number of independent studies, the analysis of each study, and how performance was summarized. Your [assumptions report](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=question) can bring the clinical justification and these computational details together. Each saved result should retain the inputs used to produce it; changed controls require a new calculation or simulation.

### Additional records for complex designs {#complex-design-record .advanced-heading .unnumbered}

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>Additional records for complex designs</summary>

For the [testing strategies in Chapter 8](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), the protocol and SAP should also specify the following items where relevant [@iche91998; @fdamultiple2022; @fdaadaptive2019; @umcgsap]:

- The primary and key secondary outcomes, treatment comparisons, success rule and family of confirmatory claims, including their testing order and error-control procedure.
- The number and timing of interim analyses, information used, efficacy or futility boundaries, safety review arrangements and who has access to unblinded results and makes decisions.
- The sample-size re-estimation or other adaptation rule, its trigger and limits, and the corresponding final testing and estimation methods.
- Maximum and expected sample sizes under stated scenarios, with the planning method or simulation used to evaluate false-positive probability, power and other relevant performance measures.
- The dated protocol and SAP versions, software, code and inputs needed to reproduce the decisions, and a record of any amendments and the information available when they were made.

The [UMCG SAP template](https://umcg.zenya.work/document/2f52710d-3ebc-495e-a4dc-6dee95742c78) includes sections on significance and multiplicity, interim analyses and changes from the protocol. In the [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=review), the planned analysis, software and conclusion fields can identify the design-specific plan, supporting documents and unresolved decisions. The [annotated core report](#write-a-sample-size-justification) remains a worked example for one comparison and a final analysis.

</details>

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- The report should state what was calculated, why those inputs were chosen, and how the result can be reproduced.
- One answer set supplies the concise calculation report and the supporting study plan.
- A complete report identifies per-group and total analyzable counts and recruitment targets.
- A review should check agreement between the narrative, saved calculations and planned analysis.

</div>

## Check your understanding {#check-reporting .unnumbered}

```{r quiz-reporting, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_chapter_quiz("reporting")
```

# Sample size for estimation {#estimation-planning .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Distinguish an estimate from the population quantity it describes.
- Explain confidence level, interval width and the repeated-study meaning of a confidence interval.
- Plan a sample size for a desired precision and interpret the interval clinically.
- Justify estimation using a new sample, existing data or a pilot, and report its assumptions.
:::

Estimation asks how large a population quantity is: a percentage, a mean, or a difference between groups. A confidence interval describes uncertainty around the estimate. Precision concerns the interval's width at a specified confidence level. Here, the sample size is chosen for a desired interval width.

## Estimates, confidence intervals and precision {#estimation-foundations .advanced-heading}

A sample estimate changes when different participants are sampled. A [confidence interval](#confidence-interval){.no-glossary-tooltip} uses the data and analysis assumptions to give a range describing uncertainty about the population quantity. A narrower interval indicates greater [precision](#precision){.no-glossary-tooltip}. A 95% confidence-interval procedure contains the true population value in about 95% of repeated studies when its assumptions hold.

For example, a population percentage estimated as 20% with an interval from 15% to 25% has a full width of 10 percentage points and a margin of 5 points on either side. The [full width](#full-width) and confidence level should be chosen for the decision the estimate will inform. Higher confidence or a narrower target width usually requires more observations under the same model.

The following example estimates the difference between the chronic pain treatments. Its sample size could have been chosen using power; the interval still helps describe the magnitude and uncertainty of the resulting comparison. CONSORT recommends reporting treatment-effect estimates with their precision [@consortee2025].

## Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval {#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically .advanced-heading}

To interpret one trial, you can compare its confidence interval with both zero and the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold introduced for the chronic pain trial. Zero represents no population difference; the clinical threshold represents the between-group benefit judged worthwhile in this example.

The estimated difference summarizes the treatment comparison. The confidence interval for this between-group difference shows uncertainty around the estimate under the analysis assumptions. At the same confidence level, a narrower interval gives a more precise estimate. Three hypothetical 95% intervals illustrate the possible clinical conclusions:

```{r clinical-intervals, echo=FALSE}
clinical_intervals <- data.frame(
  lower_pp = c(2, -8, 22),
  upper_pp = c(28, 32, 42),
  interpretation = c(
    "Evidence of benefit; its clinical importance remains uncertain. The interval excludes zero and includes benefits below and above the 20-point threshold.",
    "An inconclusive comparison. Some harm, no difference, small benefits and clinically important benefits remain compatible with the data.",
    "The interval supports a benefit above the clinical threshold. All values in the interval exceed 20 percentage points, under the analysis assumptions."),
  plot_label = c("Benefit; clinical\nimportance uncertain",
    "Inconclusive\ncomparison", "Benefit above\nclinical threshold"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `Interval for the difference in relief` = paste(clinical_intervals$lower_pp,
    "to", clinical_intervals$upper_pp, "percentage points"),
  `Clinical conclusion and explanation` = clinical_intervals$interpretation,
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Hypothetical 95% intervals for novel minus standard treatment, compared with zero and a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold.")
```

Figure \@ref(fig:clinical-interval-plot) places the intervals in Table \@ref(tab:clinical-intervals) on the same scale. Positive differences favor the novel treatment. You can see whether each interval crosses zero, crosses the clinical threshold, or lies entirely above it.

```{r clinical-interval-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Three hypothetical 95% confidence intervals on a common scale. The solid vertical line marks no between-group difference; the dashed line marks the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold. Each horizontal bar spans the stated interval limits.", fig.alt="Three horizontal confidence intervals for novel minus standard treatment. The interval from 2 to 28 percentage points excludes zero but crosses the clinical threshold of 20. The interval from minus 8 to 32 crosses both zero and 20. The interval from 22 to 42 lies entirely above 20."}
par(mar = c(5, 9.1, 4.3, 1), las = 1, bg = "white",
  fg = "#26343d", col.axis = "#26343d", col.lab = "#26343d")
plot(NA, xlim = c(-12, 48), ylim = c(.55, 3.55),
  xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
interval_rows <- 3:1
abline(h = interval_rows, col = "#e5e9ec", lwd = 1)
abline(v = 0, col = "#4b5560", lwd = 1.5)
abline(v = 20, col = "#72428b", lwd = 1.8, lty = 2)
axis(1, at = seq(-10, 40, 10), cex.axis = .95)
mtext("Difference in pain-relief percentages", side = 1, line = 2.4)
mtext("Novel minus standard treatment (percentage points)", side = 1,
  line = 3.6, cex = .85)
text(c(0, 20), 3.67, c("No difference\n0", "Clinical threshold\n20"),
  adj = c(.5, 0), cex = .85, xpd = NA)
text(-14, interval_rows, clinical_intervals$plot_label,
  adj = 1, cex = .9, xpd = NA)
segments(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, interval_rows,
  clinical_intervals$upper_pp, interval_rows,
  col = "#17658a", lwd = 3, lend = "butt")
for (limits in list(clinical_intervals$lower_pp, clinical_intervals$upper_pp)) {
  segments(limits, interval_rows - .09, limits, interval_rows + .09,
    col = "#17658a", lwd = 2)
  text(limits, interval_rows + .19, labels = limits, cex = .85)
}
```

For a 95% confidence interval and its corresponding two-sided test, an interval that excludes zero indicates statistical significance at the 5% level. Clinical interpretation also depends on whether the interval lies below, crosses, or lies entirely above the clinical threshold.

These intervals concern the population-level difference between groups; see [Between-group differences and individual benefit](#between-group-differences) for the implications for individual patients.

Across repeated studies, about 95% of intervals calculated with a 95% confidence-interval method would contain the true population difference, if the assumptions hold. The estimation activities explore how intervals vary across repeated samples. Clinical interpretation also considers harms, burden, and the credibility of the study [@sandoval2025].

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-confidence-probability">
<summary>Common misconception: this interval has a 95% probability of containing the true difference</summary>

The true population difference is fixed, while the interval changes from sample to sample. The 95% describes how often the method produces an interval containing that difference across repeated studies.

</details>

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-power-precision">
<summary>Common misconception: high power guarantees clinically useful precision</summary>

A study can detect a difference from zero while leaving considerable uncertainty about whether the benefit is clinically worthwhile. Power concerns the testing decision; precision concerns the interval's width. You can consider both when deciding whether the study can answer the clinical question.

</details>

## Estimation with a precision target {#plan-for-precision .advanced-heading}

The rehabilitation study aims to estimate the difference in mean improvement between two independent groups. You should specify how narrow the confidence interval needs to be to support a useful interpretation. Here, a 95% confidence interval with an anticipated full width of 4 score units is the precision target [@wang2020; @lakens2022].

With an assumed common SD of 5 units, the [mean-difference estimation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision) finds the smallest group size meeting this target. The calculation uses the confidence level, SD and desired width. For the simulation only, the population mean difference is set to 3 units so you can compare each interval with a known value.

```{r precision-plan}
# Define the population used in the simulation and the desired precision.
# The mean difference of 3 supplies a known truth for checking coverage.
precision_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "means", delta = 3, sd = 5,
  threshold = 2, width_target = 4, B = 5000, seed = 20260922)
# Choose the smallest group size meeting the expected interval-width target.
precision_spec$n <- plan_n(precision_spec, goal = "precision")
c(per_group = precision_spec$n,
  anticipated_full_width = anticipated_width(precision_spec))
# Repeated samples produce different estimates and interval widths.
precision_batch <- simulate_trials(precision_spec)
```

```{r precision-plan-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Analyzable per group`=precision_spec$n, `Anticipated full interval width`=round(anticipated_width(precision_spec),2),check.names=FALSE), caption="Group size required for a 95% confidence interval with anticipated full width of at most 4 score units, assuming SD 5.")
```

For normal data, this calculation uses the expected full width of a t-based interval. Realized interval widths vary with the sample SD. The simulation shows how often intervals contain the known population difference and how often their width meets the chosen target [@sandoval2025].

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

In [Activity: Estimate a mean difference with a precision target](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=mean_precision), what does a full-width target of 4 units mean? Will every simulated interval meet it?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-precision-versus-power">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A full width of 4 units corresponds to a margin of approximately 2 units on either side of the estimated difference. With SD 5, the calculation requires `r precision_spec$n` analyzable patients per group. It meets an anticipated-width target. Individual intervals can be wider or narrower because the sample SD varies across studies.

</details>
:::

## Estimate one proportion: a prevalence survey {#prevalence .advanced-heading}






A prevalence survey estimates one population proportion at a defined time. Each participant contributes a binary outcome to one sample; you choose its size for a useful [margin of error](#margin-of-error).

Such estimates can inform service planning or recruitment and retention assumptions for a future trial. The planning question is how precisely the study should estimate the population percentage [@pourhoseingholi2013; @ying2025].

Suppose a service wants to estimate the percentage of eligible patients reporting a symptom. It wants a 95% confidence interval with an approximate margin of error of 5 [percentage points](#percentage-points): half-width $d=0.05$, or a full width of 10 percentage points. This is a simple independent-sample prevalence example. Here, n is the total number of participants in a single sample.

For an anticipated population proportion $p_0$, the normal approximation gives:

\begin{equation}
n\approx\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}^{2}p_0(1-p_0)}{d^2}.
(\#eq:single-proportion)
\end{equation}

Here $p_0$ is the anticipated population proportion used to plan the study. If comparable evidence suggests a prevalence of 20% ($p_0=0.20$), the approximate requirement is 246 completed observations. If there is no useful prior estimate, 50% ($p_0=0.50$) gives the largest value of $p_0(1-p_0)$ and an approximate requirement of 385.

```{r single-proportion-precision}
# Plan for a full width of 10 percentage points at 95% confidence.
prevalence_known <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95)
# unknown_p = TRUE uses 50%, the conservative value for this approximation.
prevalence_unknown <- proportion_precision_plan(p = .20,
  full_width = .10, confidence = .95, unknown_p = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Prior estimate 20%", "Unknown: use 50% for planning"),
  `Assumed population percentage` = percent(c(prevalence_known$planning_p,
    prevalence_unknown$planning_p)),
  `Completed observations` = c(prevalence_known$n, prevalence_unknown$n),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Approximate prevalence sample sizes for a 95% interval with a 5-percentage-point margin of error.")
```

The conservative 50% choice concerns absolute precision for one proportion under this approximation. It is not a general substitute for unknown control and treatment percentages in a power calculation. For a rare outcome, an absolute margin of five percentage points might be unhelpfully wide; event counts and the chosen interval method also matter.

[Activity: Estimate a percentage with useful precision](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=prevalence). You can compare margins of error of 5 and 2.5 percentage points. The latter requires about four times as many completed observations under the formula. The app shows a Wilson interval for an illustrative realized sample; its width can differ from the planning approximation. No formula here guarantees that every realized interval meets the target. Representative recruitment matters as well: a larger convenience sample does not automatically remove selection bias [@whitley2002; @wang2020].




The worked survey illustrates one planning method. The table below places it alongside treatment comparisons and other research objectives.

## Reuse an existing dataset for a different question {#dataset-reuse .advanced-heading}

An existing dataset is another fixed-resource setting, common in bachelor projects. Suppose a completed chronic pain trial included 200 patients and also recorded sleep difficulty before treatment. Your new question is: what percentage of these trial participants reported sleep difficulty at baseline? This differs from the trial's original question about treatment effectiveness.

Baseline sleep information is available for 180 participants; 72 reported difficulty. The observed percentage is 72/180 = 40%. With the sample already fixed, the planning task is to assess the precision the available data can provide.

```{r reused-dataset}
# Estimate a percentage and interval from 72 events among 180 observations.
sleep_result <- single_proportion_interval(events = 72, n = 180,
  confidence = .95)
sleep_result
```

```{r reused-dataset-summary, echo=FALSE}
sleep_limits <- wilson_interval(.40, 180)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Measure = c("Patients in the dataset", "With baseline sleep information",
    "Reporting sleep difficulty", "Observed percentage", "95% Wilson confidence interval"),
  Result = c("200", "180", "72", "40.0%",
    paste(percent(sleep_limits[1, 1]), "to", percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])))),
  caption = "A new descriptive question answered using an existing chronic pain trial dataset.")
```

The interval describes sampling uncertainty under the model. Possible differences between the 20 patients with missing information and those who answered require separate assessment. The trial's eligibility criteria also restrict whom these results describe: its participants may not represent all patients with chronic pain. Random allocation supports the original treatment comparison.

The new question needs its own assessment of adequacy. You should check that the required variables and time points are available, that reuse is permitted, and that the analysis fits the new objective. For a new association question, you would also need to consider confounding and the relevant model. The estimate, interval and limitations should guide interpretation; observed post hoc power adds no evidence about the same result [@lakens2022; @consortee2025].

Before examining the new results, your report should document why the sample is fixed and what precision would be useful. The available sample sets the resource limit. Its adequacy depends on the precision required for the new question. For a comparison, you can evaluate independently justified differences at that fixed sample size; for this descriptive question, you can examine the attainable interval width. If it is too wide for the intended decision, you should narrow the claim or explain that more data would be needed. Your report should identify analyses developed after examining the data as exploratory.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

For your adapted research question, your plan should identify the new outcome, target population, available sample and missing observations. Would an interval of this width answer your project question? Your report should record these decisions in the [Activity: Develop and justify your study plan](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=assumptions_report), using a fixed-resource estimation goal.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-existing-data">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The new outcome is baseline sleep difficulty. The results directly describe the population defined by the original trial's eligibility criteria. The dataset contains 200 patients, with sleep information for 180 and missing information for 20. Among those with information, 72/180 = 40% reported difficulty; the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 1])` to `r percent(sleep_limits[1, 2])`.

Whether this precision is useful depends on a decision specified for the project. It may support a broad descriptive estimate, but would not support a requirement to estimate the percentage within 2 percentage points. The report should explain the fixed sample, missing information and restricted population. Adequacy here depends on precision for the descriptive objective.

</details>

:::

## Planning a pilot or feasibility study {#pilot-feasibility .advanced-heading}

So far, feasibility has meant whether you can carry out an informative main study. A preliminary pilot or feasibility study has its own research objectives: investigating whether recruitment, retention, delivery, or other procedures will work. Its sample size should support those decisions.

Suppose a team wants to test a new rehabilitation pathway and needs evidence about recruitment and follow-up. It can recruit 40 patients over three months to investigate these procedures.

You can start with systematic reviews, relevant previous studies, routine service data and clinical expertise. Your report should record the population, outcome, time point and uncertainty of each source. You should agree the main trial's clinically meaningful outcome with patients and clinicians. The pilot can investigate recruitment and retention, measurement procedures, acceptability and variability. Planning the definitive trial should combine these findings with relevant external evidence [@albers2018].

For the pilot, your plan should connect the available resources with the precision needed for these feasibility decisions. The [single-proportion example](#prevalence) explains the corresponding interval-width calculation. Here the hypothetical cap is 40 participants, and expected completion of follow-up is 80%. If 32 of 40 complete follow-up, what would that tell the team about retention?

```{r pilot-retention}
# Estimate retention and its interval from 32 completions among 40 participants.
pilot_retention <- single_proportion_interval(events = 32, n = 40,
  confidence = .95)
pilot_retention
```

```{r pilot-retention-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Completed follow-up`="32/40 (80%)", `95% Wilson confidence interval`=paste(percent(pilot_retention$lower), "to", percent(pilot_retention$upper)), check.names=FALSE), caption="Retention and its uncertainty in a 40-participant feasibility study.")
```

The observed 80% retention still has a wide interval. You can compare it with a prospectively agreed progression criterion and consider reasons for missing outcomes. A point estimate of 80% alone cannot establish that the main trial will retain at least 80%.

Your pilot size should reflect the decision it must support. Ying and colleagues distinguish estimating feasibility with useful precision, assessing progression criteria, detecting practical problems and informing variability for the main trial [@ying2025]. You should specify each outcome's denominator: retention concerns participants enrolled, while a recruitment percentage may concern eligible people approached. Forty enrolled patients do not supply forty observations for every feasibility outcome.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

Before seeing retention results, your feasibility plan should specify an unacceptable level, a desirable level and what would lead to proceeding, amending or stopping. You can compare the intervals for 40 and 80 participants. Your explanation should address whether either sample supplies useful information for those decisions, alongside acceptability and reasons for missing follow-up. The progression criteria should have a clinical and operational justification.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-pilot-progression">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

One possible set of prospectively specified criteria would treat retention below 70% as unacceptable and 80% as desirable. A team could proceed if the estimate is at least 80%, the lower 95% confidence limit exceeds 70%, and delivery and acceptability are satisfactory; amend the pathway if the interval still includes unacceptable retention; and stop or substantially redesign it if the interval lies below 70%. These illustrative thresholds and rules need clinical and operational justification before the results are seen.

For 32/40 retained participants, the 95% Wilson interval is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 40)[1, 2])`; for 64/80 it is `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 80)[1, 1])` to `r percent(wilson_interval(.80, 80)[1, 2])`. The 40-person result would lead to amendment or further investigation under these illustrative rules. The 80-person result just meets the numerical progression rule using the unrounded lower limit, but the reasons for missing follow-up and acceptability would still matter. Neither result establishes that true retention is at least 80%. Recruiting 80 would also need its own feasible time and resource plan.

</details>

:::

For another objective, suppose a practical problem independently affects 10% of participants. The probability of observing at least one problem in $n$ participants is $1-(1-0.10)^n$; 29 give at least a 95% probability. Much rarer problems require larger samples for reliable detection. A problem can remain undetected in a small pilot [@ying2025]. Different pilot objectives can therefore imply different numbers.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-pilot-goal">
<summary>Common misconception: every pilot needs a treatment-effect power calculation</summary>

A pilot may primarily investigate recruitment, retention or whether procedures are workable. The sample size should support the feasibility questions and provide useful precision for the intended decisions. Planning the definitive trial should combine the pilot findings with relevant external evidence [@albers2018].

</details>

[Activity: Pilot study: estimate retention](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pilot_feasibility). It starts with a fixed total of 40 and anticipated retention of 80%. You can compare illustrative intervals at 40 and 80 observations; make clear whether another recruitment period or collaboration could obtain the larger sample.

The app can generate one hypothetical retention count from the assumed 80% probability. It will not necessarily produce exactly 32 of 40. Both retained and non-retained participants contribute to the retention estimate when their status is known.

Before writing the protocol, you should check relevant guidance and the current funder's requirements. For examples, [NIHR HTA guidance on feasibility and pilot studies](https://njl-admin.nihr.ac.uk/document/download/2023130) distinguishes feasibility questions from definitive efficacy questions; this is an archived guidance example. The [CONSORT extension for randomized pilot and feasibility trials](https://www.bmj.com/content/355/bmj.i5239) asks for a rationale for pilot numbers and criteria for progression [@nihrfeasibility; @eldridge2016]. Reporting guidance helps you document the design. The sample size method should match the study question and planned analysis.

## Reporting an estimation-based sample size {#estimation-report .advanced-heading}

An estimation plan identifies the population quantity, outcome and assessment time, confidence level, desired full interval width, anticipated percentages or SD, interval method, software and participant counts. Its justification explains why the chosen width would be useful. For existing data, it describes the available count and anticipated precision. The [study-plan activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/assumptions_report/?stage=calculation) displays these fields when an estimation goal is selected; [Chapter 4](#reporting) explains the common report structure.

<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- An estimate describes a population quantity using sample data; its confidence interval expresses uncertainty.
- A precision target specifies confidence level and interval width.
- Estimation can concern a single population or a between-group difference.
- The justification should explain why the interval width supports the intended decision.

</div>

## Check your understanding {#check-estimation .unnumbered}

```{r quiz-estimation, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
render_chapter_quiz("estimation-planning")
```

# Exploring power and uncertain assumptions {#curves .advanced-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this chapter, you should be able to:

- Read power curves under specified population assumptions.
- Compare required sample sizes with performance at a fixed sample size.
- Assess recruitment limits and smaller plausible treatment differences.
- Assess the evidence and uncertainty behind expectations, clinical judgments and the calculation target.
- Explain how observed significance boundaries and sampling distributions relate to power.

:::

The chronic pain calculation uses one set of assumptions. What if the true benefit is smaller, or recruitment limits the number of patients? Power curves show how the answer changes.

## Activity: Chronic pain: explore power and recruitment {#activity-2-can-the-feasible-study-answer-the-question .advanced-heading}

The curves compare the expected performance of studies with different sample sizes. At any chosen sample size, each curve gives power for a different assumed true treatment difference. Chapter 11 of @superpowerbook2022 motivates examining power across a range of sample sizes and effects. Here you keep the plan for the chronic pain trial fixed and examine true control relief of 30% with treatment relief of 45%, 50% or 60%. These curves explore performance if reality differs from the planning assumption.

Suppose the clinic can recruit 200 patients in total, with 10% expected loss in each arm. This corresponds to 100 recruited and an expected 90 analyzable patients per group. Actual retention varies.

```{r curve-settings}
# Define the population assumptions and the fixed 90-patient analysis count.
curve_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 90,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, threshold = .20,
  width_target = .20)
# Compare three true differences: 15, 20 and 30 percentage points.
effect_sizes <- c(.15, .20, .30)
target_power <- .90
recruitment_cap <- 200
expected_loss <- .10
# Split total recruitment equally, allow for losses, and round down.
analyzable_cap <- floor(recruitment_cap / 2 * (1 - expected_loss))
```

```{r power-curves, fig.cap="Power for treatment differences of 15, 20 and 30 percentage points. Dashed lines show 90% target power and the recruitment limit of 90 analyzable patients per group.", fig.alt="Three curves show that smaller treatment benefits need more patients. A horizontal line marks 90 percent power and a vertical line marks 90 analyzable patients per group."}
# seq(5, 200, 5) generates counts from 5 to 200 in steps of 5.
# Calculate power at each count for each of the three differences.
curve_table <- power_curve_data(curve_spec, effect_sizes, seq(5, 200, 5))
# Draw the curves and reference lines for target power and the recruitment cap.
plot_power_curves(curve_table, target_power, analyzable_cap)
```

```{r cap-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cap_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(effect_sizes, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  data.frame(absolute_benefit = effect,
    analyzable_per_group = analyzable_cap,
    approximate_power_at_cap = spec_power(x, analyzable_cap),
    per_group_for_target = plan_n(x, target_power = target_power))
}))
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(cap_results, "approximate_power_at_cap",
  points = "absolute_benefit"),
  format = if (knitr::is_html_output()) "html" else "latex",
  col.names = c("True difference (percentage points)", "Analyzable patients per group",
    "Power with 90 per group", "Patients per group for 90% power"),
  caption = "Power with 90 patients per group and sample size needed for 90% power.")
```

## Hold sample size fixed and vary the effect {.advanced-heading}

Figure \@ref(fig:effect-curve) answers a different question: with 90 analyzable patients per group, how does power change across possible treatment benefits? The target-power crossing describes a detectable effect at that target.

```{r effect-curve, fig.cap="Approximate power across true treatment benefits with 90 analyzable patients per group and 30% control relief. The horizontal reference marks 90% power.", fig.alt="Power rises with the assumed positive treatment benefit; the horizontal reference is 90 percent power."}
# Vary the true difference from 0 to 40 points in half-point steps.
effect_grid <- seq(0, .40, .005)
# Copy the scenario, change treatment probability, and calculate power.
# vapply() returns one number for each difference; numeric(1) specifies this.
effect_power <- vapply(effect_grid, function(effect) {
  x <- curve_spec; x$p_treatment <- x$p_control + effect
  spec_power(x)
}, numeric(1))
# Plot the difference in percentage points, with power labeled as a percentage.
plot(effect_grid * 100, effect_power, type = "l", lwd = 2,
  col = "#176675", ylim = c(0, 1), yaxt = "n",
  xlab = "Absolute treatment benefit (percentage points)", ylab = "Power (%)")
axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, .2), labels = paste0(seq(0, 100, 20), "%"))
# Add a dashed horizontal line at the target power.
abline(h = target_power, lty = 2)
```

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-detection-boundary">
<summary>Common misconception: the target-power crossing is a detection boundary</summary>

An effect below the target-power crossing can still produce a significant result; an effect above it can still go undetected. Each point on the curve gives the probability of detecting the specified difference across repeated studies. The [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) is a separate judgment.

</details>

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

Predict. Which effect assumption is most demanding at the same power target?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curves-predict">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The 15-percentage-point difference requires the largest sample for the same power target, followed by 20 points and then 30 points. With control relief fixed at 30% and the analysis and error targets unchanged, smaller differences are harder to distinguish from [sampling variability](#sampling-variability). This comparison concerns true treatment differences.

</details>

The [Activity: Chronic pain: explore power and recruitment](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) assesses what a fixed recruitment limit could establish across plausible treatment differences.

The curves in *Explore assumptions* are calculated from the planning formulas. They help you choose scenarios worth investigating. With advanced controls visible, *Custom effect or variability* lets you specify control relief of 30% and treatment relief of 50% or 45% while retaining 90 patients per group. The sensitivity table updates immediately; *Simulate many studies* then estimates performance from generated patient outcomes for the selected scenario.

Explain. Which assumptions make the target feasible?

How do you distinguish 200 recruited patients from 180 expected analyzable patients?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curve-assumptions">
<summary>Model answer</summary>
