The displayed plan reaches 90% power at the 30-point target difference with 90 analyzable patients per group, given 30% standard-treatment relief, the chosen test and a 5% [Type I error probability](#alpha). It does not reach that power target for the smaller 20-point clinical threshold or the 15-point alternative. The recruitment limit is 200 people; applying 10% expected loss gives 180 expected analyzable outcomes, or 90 per group. Feasibility therefore depends on the treatment difference and event probabilities being credible, the analysis being appropriate and retention being close to its assumption. Actual recruitment, retention and study results will vary.

</details>


Justify. Write three sentences describing what the clinic's recruitment limit could establish. Do not increase the assumed benefit merely to make the design affordable.

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-curves-justify">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Recruiting 200 patients with 10% expected loss gives 180 expected analyzable patients, or 90 per group. At that count, approximate power is `r percent(cap_results$approximate_power_at_cap[3])` for a true 30-point difference and `r percent(cap_results$approximate_power_at_cap[2])` for a true 20-point difference, so the plan meets the 90% target at 30 points but not at the smaller clinical threshold. If high power at 20 percentage points is essential, the recommendation should consider more recruitment or a revised objective, acknowledging uncertainty in retention.

</details>
:::

## Comparing planning assumptions {#compare-planning-assumptions .advanced-heading}



The recruitment allowance uses one set of assumptions. A [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis){.no-glossary-tooltip} examines what happens when those assumptions change within plausible ranges. It can answer two questions:

- Before choosing your sample size: how many patients would be needed under different plausible assumptions? Here, sample size changes.
- After choosing a sample size: how would this same study perform if the true difference were smaller or variability were greater? Here, sample size stays fixed.

The next table shows both answers. Its required-count column recalculates the sample size at the clinical threshold, target difference and difference observed in previous data. Its power column keeps the original planned sample fixed. The 20-, 30- and 40-point values belong to this example; the three roles can share a value and have no fixed order. In the [sample size reasoning app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves), *Reality may differ from the plan* lets you explore this second question [@cook2018delta2; @lakens2022].

```{r pain-target-sensitivity, echo=FALSE}
pain_target_n <- ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = .60, p2 = .30,
  sig.level = .05, power = .90, alternative = "two.sided",
  strict = TRUE)$n)
pain_alternatives <- c(.50, .60, .70)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `True novel-treatment relief` = percent(pain_alternatives),
  `Difference from 30% standard-treatment relief` = paste(c(20, 30, 40), "percentage points"),
  `Required per group for 90% power` = vapply(pain_alternatives,
    function(p) ceiling(power.prop.test(p1 = p, p2 = .30,
      sig.level = .05, power = .90, alternative = "two.sided",
      strict = TRUE)$n), numeric(1)),
  `Power at the original sample size` = percent(vapply(pain_alternatives,
    function(p) power.prop.test(n = pain_target_n, p1 = p, p2 = .30,
      sig.level = .05, alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)$power,
    numeric(1))), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("Chronic-pain sensitivity: alternative required counts and approximate power with the original", pain_target_n, "patients per group held fixed."))
```

This comparison keeps standard-treatment relief at 30%, the Type I error probability at 5%, and the analysis unchanged. Your report should record why the alternatives are plausible and which uncertainty matters most for the decision. You can also vary the standard-treatment probability where relevant: the same difference at different event probabilities need not require the same sample. The continuous-outcome example below illustrates the corresponding role of variability.

```{r fixed-plan-sensitivity}
# Keep the selected sample size; vary the true difference or SD.
plan <- study_spec(outcome = "means", n = ceiling(t_plan$n), delta = 3, sd = 5)
smaller <- plan; smaller$delta <- 1
more_variable <- plan; more_variable$sd <- 7
scenarios <- list(plan, smaller, more_variable)
# Compare power and anticipated interval width under each scenario.
# vapply() extracts or calculates one numeric result per scenario.
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Scenario = c("Target difference", "Smaller true difference", "Larger standard deviation"),
  `Analyzable patients per group` = vapply(scenarios, function(x) x$n, numeric(1)),
  Power = percent(vapply(scenarios, spec_power, numeric(1))),
  `Expected full interval width (score units)` = vapply(scenarios, anticipated_width, numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE),
  digits = 3, caption = "Continuous-outcome sensitivity with the sample selected for 90% target power held fixed.")
```

## Evidence, expectations and uncertainty {#st01-expectations .advanced-heading}

Your assumptions should explain why previous findings apply to the planned study. Four questions help connect that evidence to the calculation [@cook2018delta2; @cook2019delta2]:

- What would happen with the comparator? Disease severity, background care and follow-up can change the control event percentage or outcome variability. Where data are sparse, expert judgment should be identified and its uncertainty examined.
- What could explain an apparent treatment advantage? In observational comparisons, differences in patients, care or diagnosis can contribute to the observed difference. Earlier diagnosis can lengthen measured survival without postponing death; more detailed staging can change which patients are compared within a disease stage.
- What additional benefit would justify the intervention? Patients and clinicians should consider adverse effects, treatment burden and alternatives when judging a clinically worthwhile difference. More demanding treatment may require a larger benefit to justify its use.
- How sensitive is the decision to uncertainty? Plausible ranges should reflect differences between studies and limitations in the evidence. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) shows their implications for required sample size or performance at a fixed count.

The ST01 gastric-cancer surgery trial illustrates these judgments. Its design team used a consensus estimate of 20% five-year survival with conventional (D1) surgery. Apparent advantages of more extensive (D2) surgery in Japanese observational studies could partly reflect earlier diagnosis, more detailed staging, or differences in patients' age and fitness. D2 also carried additional postoperative risks, so the anticipated survival gain needed to justify these harms [@fayers2000beliefs]. The table distinguishes the calculation target from expectations and clinical judgments elicited from 26 surgeons before recruitment.

| Planning role | Reported value and basis |
|:--|:--|
| Anticipated difference | The wider survey anticipated a 9.4-percentage-point survival advantage; the three design-committee surgeons anticipated 13.1 points. |
| Target difference | The detailed calculation used 13.5 points, from 20% to 33.5% survival, giving 400 patients at 90% power. It reflected the design committee's expectations. |
| Clinical importance | The wider survey's average interval of clinical indecision was 4.6–10.8 points. Its upper boundary represented sufficient benefit to favor D2, given the operation's additional risks. Individual judgments varied. |

Table: (\#tab:st01-planning-roles) ST01 planning roles: absolute between-group differences in five-year survival, expressed in percentage points [@fayers2000beliefs].

The survey left the original design unchanged; its clinical boundaries summarize individual surgeons' judgments. Reproducing ST01 requires its survival-analysis method. More generally, differences in patients or care may change the assumed outcomes, while treatment harms inform what benefit is worthwhile. The sample-size consequences depend on those resulting inputs and the chosen analysis.

<span id="planning-uncertainty"></span>

Uncertainty remains even when assumptions are carefully justified. In a review of 107 randomized trials, the median standardized target effect was 0.30, compared with a median observed effect of 0.11 [@rothwell2018targets]. Differences between targets and results can reflect uncertain treatment effects and sampling variability. Assessing investigator optimism also requires evidence about beliefs and their uncertainty before results are known [@liu2024uncertainty].

@benjamin2022forecasts collected forecasts from 740 principal investigators. Among the 104 trials with primary outcome results available, the mean predicted probability of a statistically significant result favoring the intervention was 59.6%; 43.3% produced one. The 16.7% survey response rate and incomplete follow-up limit generalization. These forecasts concern overall trial success; statistical power is conditional on specified assumptions. A separate review of 385 phase III oncology trials found clinical-data justification for effect assumptions in only 41 (10.6%), reinforcing the importance of documenting the evidence [@noticewala2025effects].

For your study, earlier observations and elicited expectations can inform a plausible range of population differences. Their values, the target difference and the clinical threshold can coincide or follow a different order. The chosen target needs evidence of plausibility and clinical importance. When a target exceeds the benefit supported by the evidence, your justification should examine power at smaller plausible differences. A [sensitivity analysis](#compare-planning-assumptions) makes these implications visible [@cook2018delta2].

## What can the available sample establish? {#available-sample .advanced-heading}

After accounting for expected losses, your recruitment period, funding, or available records may impose a fixed analyzable sample. You can use that count to assess power across independently justified treatment differences and the precision anticipated under the planned analysis. The [clinical interpretation of an interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) helps you judge whether the remaining uncertainty would matter for the intended decision.

For the chronic pain trial, a cap of 200 recruits with 10% expected loss gives an expected 180 analyzable patients, or 90 per group under equal recruitment and retention. The [power-curve activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_curves) evaluates this fixed count at the target difference and smaller plausible benefits. A recruitment cap limits what is available; the research objective determines whether that information would be useful.

If you need to estimate a quantity, you can assess the attainable interval width at that fixed count, using the [precision-planning principles](#plan-for-precision). The available data may support a broad description while leaving a more demanding decision unresolved. Your justification should state the resource limit and the conclusions the study could reasonably support.

## A fixed total of 70 patients {#a-fixed-total-of-70-patients .advanced-heading}

Suppose only 70 patients can be recruited in total. What power and [precision](#precision) could the study achieve after expected losses, and what conclusions could it reasonably support? Your answer should specify the research question, assumed outcomes, losses and analysis before assessing the available sample. You can then justify the proposed study or explain how a revised design or narrower objective would make the available information useful.

## Sensitivity analysis for a fixed sample size {#sensitivity-is-not-observed-post-hoc-power .advanced-heading}

These curves specify hypothetical effects before interpreting a realized study.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-observed-power">
<summary>Common misconception: power calculated from the observed effect explains the completed study</summary>

Substituting the study's observed effect into a power calculation adds no useful evidence about that same result. You should interpret the estimate, [confidence interval](#confidence-interval), study design and limitations instead. At a fixed sample size, power across independently justified hypothetical differences can still help describe the design's capabilities [@consortee2025; @lakens2022].

</details>

For example, suppose a completed study estimates a 1-unit improvement with a 95% confidence interval from -1 to 3, while a 2-unit benefit would matter clinically. The interval includes some harm, zero, a small benefit and a clinically important benefit. The study leaves those possibilities unresolved.

With an existing records dataset, explain why that sample is available, assess data quality and missingness, and report what its estimate and interval support. A [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis) at independently justified effects can still describe a fixed design's performance. It should not use the observed effect to create additional evidence for the same study. This distinction follows the sample size justification approach in @lakens2022; [the FAQ](#common-mistakes) gives a short retrospective-study example.


Power curves describe the planned study across repeated samples. The next examples examine how an individual result becomes statistically significant and how the rejection rule produces the error probabilities used in planning.

## Does the pilot already answer the clinical question? {#critical-observed-difference .advanced-heading}

For this two-sided comparison, the p-value answers: if the treatments truly had equal population relief probabilities, how likely would the chosen test be to produce a result at least as far from equality as the one observed, in either direction? This calculation also assumes that the statistical model is appropriate. A small p-value provides evidence against equal population relief probabilities under the statistical model.

The pilot's observed 40-percentage-point difference exceeds the 20-percentage-point [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold). But the estimate is uncertain. Using a two-sided comparison of proportions gives a p-value of approximately 0.074. With a Type I error probability of 5%, this does not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis using the chosen test.

What would happen with one more response? You should keep standard treatment at 3 of 10 patients, but increase novel-treatment relief from 7 to 8 of 10:

```{r pain-critical-p-values, warning=FALSE}
# Compare the pilot result with one additional treatment response
pain_p_value <- function(novel, standard, n) {
  # x gives relief counts; n gives group sizes. correct = FALSE omits continuity correction.
  prop.test(
    x = c(novel, standard),
    n = c(n, n),
    alternative = "two.sided",
    correct = FALSE
  )$p.value
}

# Compare the two observed results; round p-values to three decimal places.
round(c(
  "7 versus 3" = pain_p_value(7, 3, 10),
  "8 versus 3" = pain_p_value(8, 3, 10)
), 3)
```

```{r pain-critical-p-values-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(`Novel treatment` = c("7/10 (70%)", "8/10 (80%)"), `Standard treatment` = "3/10 (30%)", `Observed difference` = c("40 percentage points", "50 percentage points"), `p-value` = formatC(c(pain_p_value(7,3,10), pain_p_value(8,3,10)), format="f", digits=3), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Pilot comparisons with seven or eight responses to the novel treatment.")
```

With 8 rather than 7 patients reporting relief, the result becomes statistically significant. For this particular comparison, the smallest observed difference giving $p<0.05$ is therefore $0.8-0.3=0.5$, or 50 [percentage points](#percentage-points).

Notice that the [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) remains 20 percentage points. What patients would consider a worthwhile improvement does not change because your pilot happens to contain only 10 patients per group.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-significance">
<summary>Common misconception: statistical significance decides whether a treatment matters</summary>

A non-significant result can remain compatible with both no effect and a worthwhile benefit. A statistically significant difference can still be too small to matter to patients. You can examine the estimated difference and its [confidence interval](#confidence-interval) against both zero and the clinical threshold.

</details>

*The calculation above uses an approximate test without continuity correction, matching the [reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many). With such small groups, an exact test may give a different result.*

### What happens if you recruit more patients? {.advanced-heading}

You can repeat this calculation for larger studies. At each sample size, the observed percentage reporting relief with standard treatment stays at 30%. The calculation identifies the smallest number reporting relief with the novel treatment that gives $p<0.05$.

```{r pain-critical-effect, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.height=5.8, fig.cap="Smallest observed improvement giving p < 0.05 at each sample size, conditional on an observed control response of 30%. The two-sided score test uses no continuity correction. Points represent attainable patient counts; connecting lines guide the eye. The hypothetical clinical threshold is 20 percentage points. Counts are analyzable patients before adjustment for dropout.", fig.alt="The smallest observed difference giving statistical significance falls from 50 percentage points at 10 patients per group to 14 at 100 per group. A horizontal line marks the clinical threshold of 20 percentage points. The pilot difference of 40 points at 10 patients per group lies below the significance threshold."}
pain_n <- seq(10, 100, by = 10)
pain_critical <- vapply(pain_n, function(n) {
  control <- as.integer(round(0.30 * n))
  treatment <- seq.int(control + 1L, n)
  p <- vapply(treatment, function(x) pain_p_value(x, control, n), numeric(1))
  min((treatment[p < 0.05] - control) / n)
}, numeric(1))

local({
  old_par <- par(mar = c(5, 5, 2, 1), las = 1)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  plot(pain_n, 100 * pain_critical, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2,
       col = "#17658A", ylim = c(0, 66), xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Analyzable patients per group (equal allocation)",
       ylab = "Observed difference in pain relief (percentage points)")
  axis(1, at = pain_n)
  abline(h = 20, col = "#A5500C", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  points(10, 40, pch = 1, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "#303A43")
  legend("topright",
         c("Smallest observed difference with p < 0.05",
           "Clinical threshold: 20 percentage points",
           "Pilot: 7/10 versus 3/10"),
         col = c("#17658A", "#A5500C", "#303A43"),
         lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(16, NA, 1),
         lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
})
```

With 20 patients per group, an observed difference of 35 percentage points is sufficient for statistical significance under these conditions. With 50 patients per group, the corresponding difference is 20 percentage points. As the sample size increases, smaller observed differences can therefore become statistically significant.

Figure \@ref(fig:pain-critical-effect) shows how the observed significance boundary changes. The dashed line shows the clinically meaningful difference chosen for this example. With a larger sample, a result can be statistically significant even when the observed difference is smaller than this clinical threshold. You therefore need to consider the size of the difference and its confidence interval when interpreting the result.

### How does this relate to power? {.advanced-heading}

The significance boundary concerns an observed result. [Power](#statistical-power) concerns the performance of the planned study: *If the true treatment difference is 30 percentage points, how likely is your study to produce a statistically significant result?*

Different samples will give different observed differences, even when the true treatment effect remains the same. Some will be larger and others smaller. A power calculation takes this variation into account. The [simulation activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) explore this probability across repeated studies.

The observed significance boundary and the true difference used to evaluate power answer different questions [@lakens2022; @superpowerbook2022]. The [clinical interpretation of the interval](#interpret-a-confidence-interval-clinically) considers whether benefits below the clinical threshold remain compatible with the data.

## Type I and Type II error probabilities as areas {#alpha-beta .advanced-heading}

This separate example uses one group to make the error probabilities easier to draw. Imagine repeatedly sampling 25 patients and calculating their mean systolic blood pressure. The curves show the distribution of sample means across repeated studies. One curve assumes a population mean of 120 mmHg; the other assumes 125 mmHg. These are sampling distributions of the mean.

[Standard deviation](#standard-deviation){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SD) describes how much individual patients differ. [Standard error](#standard-error){.no-glossary-tooltip} (SE) describes how much an estimated mean would vary if you repeated the study with new patients. If individual blood pressures have a known SD of 15 mmHg, the mean from 25 independent patients has an SE of $15/\sqrt{25}=3$ mmHg. With 100 patients, the SE falls to 1.5 mmHg. Increasing the sample size reduces the standard error of the mean while the population SD remains fixed.

For this illustration, the null hypothesis specifies a mean of 120 mmHg. A one-sided test looks for an increase, rejecting the null when the sample mean exceeds a cutoff called the critical value. The [two-arm treatment-comparison activities](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_one_many) use [two-sided tests](#two-sided-test).

Under the 120 mmHg curve, the area above the cutoff is the probability of a false positive: the [Type I error probability](#alpha). Under the 125 mmHg curve, the area below the cutoff is the probability of a false negative: the [Type II error probability](#beta). The area under the alternative curve above the cutoff is the true-positive probability, or power. Figure \@ref(fig:sampling-distribution-figure) separates the two assumed populations so that each shaded area has an unambiguous interpretation.

```{r alpha-beta-areas}
# Population means under the null and the specified alternative.
mu0 <- 120
mu1 <- 125
sigma <- 15
n <- 25
alpha <- .05
# sqrt(n) is the square root of n; the mean varies less as n increases.
standard_error <- sigma / sqrt(n)
# For this one-sided example, qnorm() gives the rejection cutoff.
critical <- mu0 + qnorm(1 - alpha) * standard_error
# pnorm() gives the probability below that cutoff under the alternative.
# This is the Type II error probability; its complement is power.
beta <- pnorm(critical, mean = mu1, sd = standard_error)
c(standard_error = standard_error, critical = critical,
  beta = beta, power = 1 - beta)
```

```{r alpha-beta-areas-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Standard error", "Critical mean", "Type I error probability", "Type II error probability", "Power"), Result=c(paste(standard_error,"mmHg"), paste(round(critical,1),"mmHg"), percent(alpha), percent(beta), percent(1-beta))),
  caption = "Error probabilities and power for the specified sampling distributions.")
```

```{r sampling-distribution-figure, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Sampling distributions of the mean with 25 independent observations and known SD 15 mmHg. In the upper panel, the shaded rejection area is Type I error probability. In the lower panel, the shaded non-rejection area is Type II error probability and the shaded rejection area is power.", fig.alt="The upper null curve is centered at 120 and the lower alternative curve at 125 mmHg. Both have standard error 3. The critical mean is about 124.9; Type I error probability is 5 percent and Type II error probability about 49 percent."}
sampling_example <- normal_sampling_operating_characteristics(
  mu0 = mu0, mu1 = mu1, sigma = sigma, n = n, alpha = alpha,
  sidedness = "greater")
plot_sample_mean_distributions(sampling_example)
```

Here the critical mean is about 124.9 mmHg and power is about 51%. Repeating the study at the specified alternative would produce a mean above that threshold about half the time.

[Activity: Explore Type I and Type II error probabilities and power](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=alpha_beta) lets you move a rejection boundary and see how false positives, false negatives and power change. You can also examine the effect of sample size.

These areas are calculated directly from a one-sample normal model with a known population SD.


<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- A power curve describes a specified analysis under explicit assumptions.
- Evidence and its uncertainty should inform expectations and the calculation target; clinical importance also needs justification.
- The power at a smaller worthwhile difference may be lower than the target power.
- A recruitment limit can leave an important benefit difficult to detect.

</div>

# Building and evaluating simulations {#simulation .advanced-heading}



::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Generate and analyze one hypothetical trial.
- Repeat the trial to assess rejection and interval coverage.
- Explain how [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error) differs from uncertainty in the planning assumptions.
- Describe how evaluating interim decisions and adaptations extends the simulation workflow.
:::

This chapter returns to the two-arm chronic pain trial and its planned analysis.

The curves in Figure \@ref(fig:power-curves) describe the performance of the chronic pain design across repeated studies. Now generate individual trials under the same assumptions to see why their estimates, intervals and decisions vary.

Simulation is especially useful when the planned analysis or dependency between observations makes a simple formula inadequate. Your simulation plan should define the quantity to estimate, justify the assumed population values, and specify the analysis. You can then generate and analyze repeated studies, summarize their performance with Monte Carlo uncertainty, and examine plausible alternative assumptions [@pargent2024]. For complex models, your report should also describe failed model fits and performance when the null hypothesis is true. A simulation is only as informative as its assumptions and implementation.

The [simulation reproducibility guide](#simulation-reproducibility) explains how the generating assumptions, repetitions, analysis and software should be documented.

## Activity: Simulate repeated chronic pain trials {#activity-3-generate-analyze-repeat-summarize .advanced-heading}

The custom-simulation approach in chapter 15 of @superpowerbook2022 starts from the planned trial and its analysis. The binary example uses the same score test as the [existing reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation).

[Activity: Simulate repeated chronic pain trials](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) to connect these four steps with one study and repeated studies in the app. The prepared batch and app use the same sample size and analysis.

This extends the core simulation: the question is now whether the analysis has useful power, confidence interval coverage and interval width under the specified population. The activity opens in *Many studies*. You can first select *One study* to follow one generated dataset through its analysis, then return to *Many studies* and run 5,000 repetitions. Each trial contains 60 patients per group; the simulation repeats that trial 5,000 times.

Figure \@ref(fig:simulation-loop) shows how these repetitions surround the generation and analysis of one trial. The population assumptions and analysis stay fixed while each repetition generates new patient outcomes.

```{r simulation-loop, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="The simulation repeats a complete trial and its analysis 5,000 times. Each trial contains 60 patients per group. Changing the patients per group changes the study design; increasing the repetitions improves the precision of the estimated simulation performance.", fig.alt="A loop connects four steps. Generate one trial with 60 patients per group under standard and novel relief probabilities of 30% and 60%. Analyze its difference, confidence interval and p-value. Repeat generation and analysis for 5,000 independent trials. Summarize power, confidence interval coverage and width across those trials."}
draw_simulation_loop()
```

### Step 1: generate one trial {.advanced-heading}

This simulation uses 60 independent patients per group, with relief probabilities of 30% and 60%. The basic planning calculation gave 56 per group; 60 is a separate illustrative sample size used consistently in this simulation and its matching activity. The true population difference assumed in this simulation is the 30-percentage-point [target difference](#target-difference). Each patient's outcome is zero (no relief) or one (relief).

```{r generate-trial}
# Fix the random-number starting point so rerunning this code reproduces the trial.
set.seed(20260921)
n <- 60
# Generate one 0/1 outcome per patient: 1 = relief, 0 = no relief.
control <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .30)
treatment <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = .60)
# sum() counts the patients with relief in each group.
c(control_relief = sum(control), treatment_relief = sum(treatment))
```

```{r generate-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Group=c("Standard treatment", "Novel treatment"), Patients=n, `Reporting relief`=c(sum(control),sum(treatment)), `Relief percentage`=percent(c(mean(control),mean(treatment))), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Observed pain relief in one simulated trial.")
```

### Step 2: apply the planned analysis {.advanced-heading}

You can use a two-sided pooled score test without continuity correction. The helper also calculates a Newcombe-Wilson interval for the risk difference [@newcombe1998]. These are different procedures: test rejection and interval exclusion of zero can occasionally disagree.

```{r analyze-trial}
# Analyze the relief counts using the tutorial's binary-outcome helper.
# The returned result includes the difference, confidence interval and p-value.
one_result <- analyse_binary(sum(treatment), sum(control), n, alpha = .05)
one_result
```

```{r analyze-trial-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Measure=c("Observed treatment difference", "95% confidence interval", "p-value", "Testing decision"), Result=c(paste(round(100*one_result$estimate,1),"percentage points"), paste(round(100*one_result$lower,1),"to",round(100*one_result$upper,1),"percentage points"), formatC(one_result$p_value,format="f",digits=3), if(one_result$p_value < .05) "Reject the zero-difference null" else "Do not reject the zero-difference null")),
  caption = "Estimated benefit and testing decision in one simulated trial.")
```

`estimate` is treatment minus control; `lower` and `upper` are confidence limits. The [p-value](#p-value) tests a zero difference. The helper's score-test p-value can be checked against R:

```{r independent-check}
# Check the helper against R's two-sided test of independent proportions.
# Group sizes are supplied twice; no continuity correction is applied.
reference <- prop.test(c(sum(treatment), sum(control)), c(n, n),
  correct = FALSE)
# Compare the two p-values; $ selects a named component of each result.
c(helper_p = one_result$p_value, R_p = reference$p.value)
```

```{r independent-check-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Tutorial helper", "R score test"), `p-value`=formatC(c(one_result$p_value,reference$p.value),format="f",digits=4), check.names=FALSE),
  caption = "Agreement between two implementations of the planned score test.")
```

This comparison checks agreement between the p-value calculations. The two functions use different confidence-interval methods. When both groups have all successes or all failures, the helper returns a p-value of one.

### Step 3: repeat independent trials {.advanced-heading}

The efficient helper generates the event count in each group directly from a binomial distribution. This is equivalent to adding up independent binary outcomes in each group. It applies the same analysis to every trial.

```{r repeat-trials}
# Specify one trial's assumptions and B = 5,000 independent repetitions.
trial_spec <- study_spec(outcome = "proportions", n = 60,
  p_control = .30, p_treatment = .60, alpha = .05,
  threshold = .20, width_target = .30, B = 5000, seed = 20260921)
# Generate and analyze all trials using the same assumptions.
trials <- simulate_trials(trial_spec)
# Display only the first four rows of the results.
head(trials$results, 4)
```

### Step 4: summarize what the design achieves {.advanced-heading}

```{r trial-summary}
# Summarize results across trials, including Monte Carlo uncertainty.
# Format the summary as a table.
knitr::kable(display_simulation_summary(simulation_summary(trials)),
  caption = "Performance across repeated studies, with Monte Carlo standard errors and 95% intervals.")
```

The percentage of statistically significant simulated results estimates [power](#statistical-power) under these assumptions. Coverage is the percentage of [confidence intervals](#confidence-interval) containing the true population difference assumed in the simulation. The percentage meeting the width target counts intervals with a full width no greater than 30 [percentage points](#percentage-points). These are three separate properties.

<details class="misconception" id="misconception-simulation-repetitions">
<summary>Common misconception: running more simulations makes the study more powerful</summary>

Increasing the number of simulated studies makes the estimated probability of a statistically significant result more precise. Increasing the patients per group changes the study; increasing the simulation repetitions improves your numerical description of it.

</details>

```{r trial-intervals, echo=FALSE, fig.height=6, fig.cap="Risk-difference confidence intervals from the first 30 simulated trials. Filled dots indicate rejection of zero. Reference lines mark the 20-percentage-point clinical threshold and the 30-percentage-point assumed population difference used for planning.", fig.alt="Intervals vary from trial to trial. Separate lines mark zero, the 20-point clinical threshold and the 30-point assumed population difference. The preceding table reports rejection, coverage and attainment of the full interval width target across all 5,000 trials."}
plot_trial_intervals(trials$results, trial_spec)
```

## Precision of a simulation {#precision-of-a-simulation .advanced-heading}

Even with unchanged assumptions, another batch of simulated trials will give a slightly different estimated power. This is [Monte Carlo error](#monte-carlo-error){.no-glossary-tooltip}: uncertainty caused by using a finite number of simulation repetitions. More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty while the number of patients in each trial stays fixed.

The core activity generated 5,000 trials at each of 20, 50 and 80 patients per group, assuming 30% and 60% relief. Returning to those trials, the following histograms count the [p-values](#p-value) from the independent simulated studies. The dashed line marks the chosen significance level. The fraction below the line estimates power under the specified alternative (Figure \@ref(fig:p-values)).

```{r p-values, echo=FALSE, fig.height=7, fig.cap="P-values from 5,000 independent clinical trials at each sample size. The percentage of p-values below the chosen significance level estimates power for the assumed relief probabilities.", fig.alt="Three histograms compare p-values with 20, 50 and 80 patients per group. The percentages of statistically significant results and their Monte Carlo intervals are in the following table."}
par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (batch in batches) plot_p_values(batch)
```

```{r simulation-monte-carlo-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(display_probabilities(power_results,
  c("simulated_power", "MC_lower_95", "MC_upper_95")),
  caption = "Estimated power and Monte Carlo intervals for the three simulated sample sizes.")
```

The observed percentage of statistically significant results summarizes the simulated studies. When the specified population difference is nonzero, it estimates power (the true-positive probability). When there is no population difference, it estimates the Type I error probability (the false-positive probability). Confidence interval coverage is the percentage of intervals containing the assumed true effect. [Monte Carlo uncertainty](#monte-carlo-error) is uncertainty from using a limited number of simulated studies. The app tables pair these established terms with their practical meaning.

A treatment-effect confidence interval describes uncertainty about the between-group difference estimated from one trial. A Monte Carlo interval describes uncertainty in the power estimated from a limited number of simulated trials. More patients can improve the precision of the treatment estimate; more simulation repetitions improve the precision of the estimated power.

Here, $n$ denotes patients per group and $B$ denotes the number of simulated studies. If $\hat p$ is the simulated rejection fraction, its approximate Monte Carlo standard error is:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{MCSE}=\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/B}.
(\#eq:mcse)
\end{equation}

With statistically significant results in 80% of simulated studies and $B=5000$, MCSE is about `r round(100 * sqrt(.8 * .2 / 5000), 2)` percentage points. The tables use Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo uncertainty. These intervals remain informative even when a simulation observes no rejections or all rejections. Increasing $B$ does not resolve uncertainty about the real treatment effect.

## Explore missing outcomes {#explore-missing-outcomes .advanced-heading}

The [repeated chronic pain trial activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) also lets you examine how missing outcomes affect a treatment comparison. Under *Explore further*, the expandable *Explore missing outcomes* controls offer four scenarios. Each uses the same recruited count and the same population relief probabilities, so you can distinguish the consequences of losing information from those of selectively losing particular outcomes.

| Scenario | Assumptions about missing outcomes |
|:--|:--|
| Complete outcomes | Every recruited participant has an observed outcome. |
| Equal losses | 10% expected loss in each group, unrelated to relief. |
| Unequal losses | 10% expected loss with standard treatment and 20% with novel treatment, unrelated to relief. |
| Outcome-related losses | The same overall expected losses of 10% and 20%; in the novel-treatment group, participants without relief are three times as likely to have missing outcomes as those with relief. |

Table: Missing-outcome scenarios in the repeated chronic pain trial activity.

This [sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity-analysis) uses hypothetical teaching assumptions. In the outcome-related scenario, the missingness probabilities are calibrated to preserve 20% expected loss in the novel-treatment group. At 60% population relief, the probabilities of a missing outcome are approximately 11.1% among those with relief and 33.3% among those without it. Actual losses vary between simulated studies. Equal recruitment is retained; group sizes after loss can differ.

In *One study*, you can see recruited, retained, and missing counts in each group, together with example participant records. The simulation shows the underlying outcomes for teaching, including those marked missing. The analysis uses only observed outcomes. In a real study, those missing outcomes would be unknown.

In *Many studies*, the mean estimated difference is compared with the known population difference; their difference estimates bias. Coverage is assessed against that same full-population difference. The table also reports retained counts, interval widths, and statistically significant results. A high significance percentage can accompany biased estimates and poor coverage. Comparisons with no observed outcomes in one group are reported as unavailable; performance summaries use the estimable comparisons.

The available-case analysis uses a two-sided pooled score test and a Newcombe-Wilson interval with the actual retained group sizes. It illustrates the consequences of a simple analysis under different missingness assumptions. Planning an appropriate missing-data analysis for a real trial requires assumptions and methods matched to the intended treatment effect [@bell2013dropout; @little2012missing]. The [recruitment discussion](#account-for-expected-losses) explains differential dropout and recruitment allowances; the [reproducibility chapter](#tutorial-methods) records the simulation procedures.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

With 60 recruited participants per group, how do unequal losses unrelated to relief compare with outcome-related losses at the same expected percentages?

What happens to the estimated difference, coverage, and significance percentage?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-missing-outcomes">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When loss is unrelated to relief, estimates should remain centered approximately on the full-population difference, although fewer observations reduce precision and can lower power. With outcome-related losses in the novel-treatment group, participants with relief are more likely to remain observed. The available-case comparison therefore tends to overestimate the benefit. With population relief of 30% and 60%, the retained novel-treatment population has approximately 66.7% relief, so the estimated difference tends toward 36.7 percentage points instead of the true 30 points. Coverage can fall even when the percentage of significant results rises. More simulation repetitions clarify these patterns; increasing recruitment reduces random uncertainty but leaves this selection bias in place.

</details>
:::

## Compare simulation with a planning approximation {.advanced-heading}

```{r simulation-benchmark}
# TRUE/FALSE rejection indicators have a mean equal to the fraction rejecting.
# Compare that simulated power with the normal planning approximation.
c(simulated_power = mean(trials$results$reject),
  approximate_planning_power = spec_power(trial_spec))
```

```{r simulation-benchmark-formatted, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Method=c("Repeated-trial simulation", "Planning approximation"), Power=percent(c(mean(trials$results$reject),spec_power(trial_spec)))),
  caption = "Power estimated by simulation and by the planning approximation.")
```

A difference can reflect Monte Carlo error or the approximation used for binary planning. Increasing the number of simulations reduces only the Monte Carlo component. Simulation evaluates the analysis under specified assumptions. Their suitability for the clinical study requires supporting evidence.

::: {.activity}
<p class="question-label">Question to consider</p>

With 60 patients per group, what happens if true treatment relief is 45% rather than 60%?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-predict">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

With control relief still at 30%, the true treatment difference falls from 30 to 15 percentage points. Across repeated trials with 60 patients per group, observed differences should center around 15 points and fewer trials should reject the [null hypothesis](#null-hypothesis). The original sample size and the 20-point [clinical threshold](#clinical-threshold) stay fixed; the true 15-point benefit is below that threshold. Individual trials can still produce significant results, which would not by itself establish a clinically worthwhile benefit.

</details>

You can explore this in the [sample size reasoning app](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) using *Custom effect or variability*. The planning probabilities stay unchanged; the population probabilities assumed for the simulation become 30% for control and 45% for treatment. The planned sample stays fixed. A further simulation with equal probabilities in both groups lets you examine false positives when there is no true difference.

Your explanation should report the assumed population probabilities, patients per group, replications, percentage of statistically significant results and its Monte Carlo interval. Your explanation should distinguish uncertainty in the simulation from uncertainty in the clinical assumptions.

```{r model-smaller-trial, include=FALSE}
model_changed_trial_spec <- trial_spec
model_changed_trial_spec$p_treatment <- .45
model_changed_simulation <- simulation_summary(simulate_trials(model_changed_trial_spec))[1, ]
```


<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-report">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For the smaller-effect scenario, the generating probabilities are 30% standard-treatment relief and 45% novel-treatment relief, with 60 patients per group and 5,000 independent simulated trials. In this prepared simulation, the percentage of statistically significant results is `r percent(model_changed_simulation$estimate)`, with a 95% Monte Carlo interval of `r percent(model_changed_simulation$MC_lower_95)` to `r percent(model_changed_simulation$MC_upper_95)`. This estimates the probability of rejecting zero under that specified 15-point true difference. The Monte Carlo interval describes uncertainty in the estimated performance caused by the finite number of simulated studies. Another simulation batch may give a slightly different estimate.

</details>


Would the original plan still answer the clinical question?

What extra evidence or design change would help?

<details class="model-answer" id="model-answer-simulation-justify">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The original plan evaluates power at a true 30-point difference. If the true difference is only 15 points, the trial has lower power to reject zero and its true benefit falls below the 20-point clinical threshold. It can still estimate the difference, but it may give an inconclusive result and a significant result would not establish that the clinical threshold has been exceeded. Better evidence on treatment response, control response and clinical importance would help assess whether the planning assumptions remain credible. A larger sample or collaboration could improve [precision](#precision) or power for an independently justified difference; adding simulation repetitions would only improve the numerical precision of the simulation estimate.

</details>
:::


## Simulating interim decisions and adaptations {#simulating-decision-rules .advanced-heading}

The examples above simulate a study with one final analysis. A design with [interim analyses or stopping guidelines](#interim-analyses-stopping) needs each simulated trial to follow its complete decision process: generate the data available at the first planned analysis, apply the relevant rule, then stop or continue. If [sample-size re-estimation](#sample-size-re-estimation) is planned, the simulation should apply that rule and the corresponding final analysis [@fdaadaptive2019].

The evaluation should include scenarios with no treatment difference to estimate false-positive probability, and plausible beneficial differences to estimate power. With [several confirmatory claims](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons), it should also consider scenarios where some null hypotheses are true and others are false. Useful summaries include the probability of stopping at each stage, the expected sample size and its distribution, and the accuracy of effect estimates and confidence intervals. These are operating characteristics: how the complete design behaves across repeated studies [@iche91998; @fdaadaptive2019].

For example, a proposed interim look in the chronic pain trial would require a simulation that includes four-week outcome availability, the stopping boundary and any recruitment already underway when a decision is made. The current [chronic pain simulation activity](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation) illustrates the fixed-sample workflow. Evaluating interim decisions requires a design-specific implementation with a statistician and the [additional reporting record](#complex-design-record).

## Evaluating the discharge calculation {#discharge-simulation .advanced-heading}

The [discharge exercise](#discharge) compares standard care at 80% with treatment at 96% or 90%, using target power of 80% or 90%. Outcomes near 100% leave few patients without the event, so the test approximation deserves closer examination.

These planning results use the same approximation as the [reasoning lab](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge). Simulated performance can help you assess whether the approximation is adequate for the proposed event probabilities and sample size.

[Activity: Discharge percentages](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=discharge) explores planning and simulated performance when the event probability is close to 100%.

This activity tests the planning approximation in a setting where few participants remain without the favorable event. After checking the plan, repeated simulations estimate the rejection probability of the specified binary test. A null scenario can also reveal whether its false-positive probability is close to the chosen 5%. Neither one simulated result nor agreement with a power target establishes that the clinical assumptions are credible.




<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Simulation generates data, applies the planned analysis, and summarizes repeated results.
- Simulated power and coverage depend on the assumed population and analysis.
- More repetitions improve the numerical precision of the simulation estimate. Evidence from relevant studies helps assess uncertainty about the population.
- Evaluating an adaptive design requires simulating its complete decision rules, including when it stops and how it changes sample size.

</div>

# Reproducibility and open science {#appendix .advanced-heading}

::: {.learning-goals .advanced-outcomes}
After this section, you should be able to:

- Explain why transparent documentation supports checking and reuse of study plans.
- Reproduce a saved calculation or simulation using its recorded inputs and software.
- Distinguish computational reproducibility from replication with new data.
- Choose software suited to the planned analysis and recognize when statistical advice is useful.
- Compare software results using matching methods and assumptions.
- Identify which methods and software settings could explain different numerical results.
:::

## Why reproducibility matters {#why-reproducibility-matters .advanced-heading}

A sample-size result is useful when another researcher can understand how it was obtained, check the calculation, and assess whether its assumptions fit the proposed study. Numerical inputs, statistical procedures, software settings and rounding rules can all affect the result. Clear documentation makes errors easier to identify and allows you to revisit the plan when new evidence becomes available.

Here, computational reproducibility means obtaining consistent results using the same inputs, computational procedures and conditions. Replicability concerns whether studies collecting new data to address the same scientific question produce consistent findings. These definitions follow @nas2019. Reproducing a calculation helps establish that its implementation can be checked. Its assumptions and the suitability of the study design still require scientific judgment.

Open science supports scrutiny and reuse by making research methods, outputs and supporting resources accessible. A shared protocol, analysis code, documented assumptions and an identified software version help others understand and build on your work. Data access should respect consent, confidentiality and other legitimate restrictions [@unesco2021]. The synthetic examples here allow you to explore and share the computational workflow without using patient records.

## Software and statistical support {#software-support .advanced-heading}

For straightforward calculations, such as comparing two independent group means or percentages, established software can help you calculate sample size and explore alternative assumptions. Your choice should reflect the study design, planned analysis, and inputs you can justify. Table \@ref(tab:software-options) summarizes options with different combinations of calculations, explanations, and graphical displays.

<details id="software-options">
<summary>Software options</summary>

| Resource | Access | Main use |
|:--|:--|:--|
| [G\*Power](https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower), [WebPower](https://webpower.psychstat.org/wiki/models/index), and [PAMLj for jamovi](https://pamlj.github.io/) | Free | Power and sample-size calculations for common statistical analyses; the available procedures differ between programs. |
| [Superpower](https://aaroncaldwell.us/SuperpowerBook/) | Free | Planning factorial experiments using means, SDs, and correlations, with simulations and accompanying explanations [@lakenscaldwell2021]. |
| [presize](https://github.com/dcr-unibe-ch/presize) | Free | Planning sample size around the desired width of a confidence interval. |
| [PASS](https://www.ncss.com/software/pass/) | Paid | Dedicated software covering a broad range of power and precision calculations, with documentation of procedures, assumptions, and worked examples [@pass2022]. |
| [nQuery](https://www.statsols.com/) | Paid | Dedicated clinical-trial planning software, including fixed, adaptive, and Bayesian designs; availability depends on the edition. |
| [Stata](https://www.stata.com/features/overview/power-and-sample-size/), [SAS](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/66103/HTML/default/statug_power_overview.htm), and [IBM SPSS Statistics](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/spss-statistics/30.0.0?topic=features-power-analysis) | Licensed statistical software | Power and sample-size procedures within an analysis environment your institution may already provide. |

Table: (\#tab:software-options) Selected software for power, sample-size, and precision planning. Available procedures depend on the program, version, and edition.

</details>

The documentation for the version you use should identify the procedure and its assumptions. Your report should record that version and the selected settings so the calculation can be checked.

Real studies often involve additional decisions. Early consultation with a statistician is especially useful when:

- observations are related, as in repeated measurements, crossover studies, or participants grouped within clinics;
- the study involves several primary outcomes, multiple comparisons, interim analyses, or non-inferiority or equivalence objectives;
- the target difference or variability is uncertain, recruitment is limited, or missing outcomes and treatment switching may affect the analysis.

Involving a statistician while the research question and protocol are still being developed can help you choose a suitable design and analysis, justify the planning assumptions, and identify information you need to collect. These decisions can prevent avoidable changes later. Clinical-trial guidance emphasizes statistical collaboration, documentation of assumptions, and investigation of their consequences [@iche91998; @cook2018delta2]. The example below illustrates why the meaning of a software input deserves the same attention as its numerical value.

### Beware of your assumptions in every calculation tool or software you use {#gpower-assumptions .advanced-heading}

Every calculation depends on the selected method and the meaning of its inputs. The [continuous-outcome example](#two-means) illustrates this using G\*Power. The target difference between group means is 3 score units, the common within-group SD is 5, allocation is equal, the two-sided Type I error probability is 5%, and target power is 90%. The difference observed in previous data remains 4 units and the clinical threshold remains 2 units.

[G\*Power](https://www.psychologie.hhu.de/arbeitsgruppen/allgemeine-psychologie-und-arbeitspsychologie/gpower) asks for different effect-size measures depending on the selected analysis [@faul2007]. For an independent-samples t test, Cohen's $d$ expresses the target difference relative to the common within-group SD:

\[
d=\frac{3}{5}=0.60.
\]

The one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) procedure asks for Cohen's $f$. It describes the spread of the group means around their overall mean, relative to the within-group SD. With two equally sized groups, a common SD and no covariate adjustment, the group means each lie half the between-group difference from their overall mean. Consequently [@gpowermanual2023]:

\[
f=\frac{d}{2}=\frac{0.60}{2}=0.30.
\]

The letter beside the effect-size field changes which value you should enter. Table \@ref(tab:gpower-effect-sizes) shows the consequence of entering $d$ in a field that expects $f$.

```{r gpower-calculation}
# Store the same mean difference, SD and statistical criteria in one list.
gpower_inputs <- list(difference = 3, sd = 5, alpha = .05, power = .90)
# Standardize the difference. For two equally sized groups only, f = d / 2.
gpower_d <- gpower_inputs$difference / gpower_inputs$sd
gpower_f <- gpower_d / 2
# Obtain the independent two-sample t-test requirement as a reference.
gpower_t_plan <- stats::power.t.test(
  delta = gpower_inputs$difference, sd = gpower_inputs$sd,
  sig.level = gpower_inputs$alpha, power = gpower_inputs$power,
  type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE)
# Calculate one-way ANOVA power for two equally sized groups.
# qf() finds the null cutoff; pf() gives the probability beyond it under the alternative.
anova_power <- function(n_per_group, f) {
  df_error <- 2 * n_per_group - 2
  pf(qf(1 - gpower_inputs$alpha, df1 = 1, df2 = df_error),
    df1 = 1, df2 = df_error, ncp = 2 * n_per_group * f^2,
    lower.tail = FALSE)
}
# Search whole-number group sizes and select the first meeting target power.
anova_n <- function(f) {
  candidates <- 2:1000
  candidates[which(anova_power(candidates, f) >= gpower_inputs$power)[1]]
}
# Compare correct f with incorrectly entering d in the f field.
gpower_correct_n <- anova_n(gpower_f)
gpower_wrong_n <- anova_n(gpower_d)
gpower_actual_power <- anova_power(gpower_wrong_n, gpower_f)
```

```{r gpower-effect-sizes, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Calculation = c("Two-sided independent-samples t test",
    "Equivalent two-group one-way ANOVA",
    "ANOVA with d mistakenly entered as f"),
  `Effect-size input` = c("Correct: d = 0.60", "Correct: f = 0.30",
    "Incorrect: f = 0.60"),
  `Analyzable per group` = c(ceiling(gpower_t_plan$n), gpower_correct_n,
    gpower_wrong_n), check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Required analyzable patients per group for a 3-unit target difference and SD 5: correctly specified effect sizes and a mistaken input. All calculations use a 5% Type I error probability, 90% target power and equal allocation.")
```

Entering $0.60$ in the $f$ field makes the software plan for a difference twice as large as intended: 6 units instead of 3. The resulting sample of `r gpower_wrong_n` patients per group would have approximately `r round(100 * gpower_actual_power)`% power to detect the intended 3-unit difference. The difference observed in previous data and clinical threshold are unchanged.

These counts were calculated in R using the corresponding noncentral t and F distributions and rounded upward to equal group sizes. They exclude recruitment losses. In G\*Power, the matching procedures are *Means: Difference between two independent means (two groups)* under *t tests*, and *ANOVA: Fixed effects, omnibus, one-way* under *F tests*. Both use an *A priori* calculation; the t test uses two tails and allocation ratio 1, while the ANOVA uses two groups.

Before using a result, you should check that the selected procedure matches the planned analysis and that each input has the meaning the software expects. Recording the target difference and SD in their original units makes the calculation easier to check. The [methods and software record](#tutorial-methods) explains what to retain.

For a planned analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), baseline adjustment introduces further assumptions about how the covariates relate to the outcome and how much variation remains after adjustment. The effect-size input should reflect that analysis. The simple $f=d/2$ conversion above applies to the stated unadjusted two-group comparison. The FDA's guidance discusses planning and prespecifying covariate adjustment [@fda2023covariates].

## Methods used in this tutorial {#tutorial-methods .advanced-heading}

The table distinguishes the planning calculation from the analysis of simulated data. Equal allocation and independent observations are assumed in the basic two-group examples. Differences are treatment minus control; their units and direction should be explicit.

| App or example | Planning or calculation procedure | Analysis or interval procedure |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Two proportions | Normal approximation using R's `stats::power.prop.test()`, two-sided with `strict = TRUE`; required patients rounded upward per group | The reasoning lab uses a two-sided pooled score test without continuity correction and a Newcombe-Wilson interval for the difference |
| Two means: introductory calculator | Normal approximation using the target difference, common SD and normal quantiles | The reasoning lab uses a pooled-variance t test and t interval; test-based planning uses `stats::power.t.test()` |
| One population percentage | Normal approximation for the requested margin of error; the unknown-percentage option uses 50% for planning | A simulated binomial count is summarized with a Wilson interval |
| Sampling distributions | Normal probabilities for one sample mean with a known population SD | Rejection boundaries and probabilities follow the selected one- or two-sided rule |
| Recruitment adjustment | Optional switching multiplier $1/(1-a-b)^2$, followed by division by each group's retained fraction; the larger requirement is rounded upward once and used in both groups | Assumes complete switching and little variance change; equal recruitment with potentially unequal expected retained counts. It calculates requirements without generating patient outcomes |

Table: Statistical procedures used by the tutorial's calculation and simulation apps.

The score test and Newcombe-Wilson interval use different constructions, so their decisions at the null need not coincide exactly. A comparison across software should match the test, interval method, sidedness, allocation, correction and rounding rules. The [statistical methods documentation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/statistical-methods.html) describes implementation details and limitations.

## How the simulations work {#simulation-reproducibility .advanced-heading}

<details class="advanced-explanation">
<summary>How the simulations work</summary>

The reporting framework ADEMP identifies the aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands (the quantities being estimated), methods and performance measures [@morris2019]. For the chronic-pain activity, these correspond to investigating study performance; generating relief outcomes at specified probabilities; estimating the between-group difference; applying the chosen test and interval; and summarizing rejection, coverage and interval width.

For one binary study, the app generates independent Bernoulli patient outcomes. For many studies, it generates binomial event counts for each group and analyzes each pair of counts. Normal-outcome studies assume independent observations with a common SD. The repeated-study implementation generates normally distributed mean differences and chi-squared pooled variances; under these assumptions, these have the same sampling distributions as the corresponding summaries of complete patient datasets.

Power is estimated by the fraction of studies with p-values below the chosen Type I error probability. Under a null scenario, that fraction estimates the false-positive probability. Interval coverage counts intervals containing the specified population value. The number of studies, Monte Carlo standard error and interval procedure should accompany simulation summaries; the apps use Wilson intervals for the simulated fractions.

The random seed, random-number generator settings and software environment help reproduce a particular simulated batch. Changing the simulation algorithm can change the realized random draws even when its statistical model is equivalent. Agreement of individual random outcomes requires the same computational procedure as well as the same assumptions.

</details>

## Software and saved records {#software-record .advanced-heading}

The missing-outcome extension uses binary relief outcomes and a fixed recruited count per group. Its four scenarios assume no loss, 10% loss in both groups, 10%/20% loss independent of relief, or 10%/20% loss with outcome-related selection in the novel-treatment group. For population relief probability $p$, overall loss $r$, and missingness risk ratio $k$ for no relief versus relief, the probabilities are $q_{\mathrm{relief}}=r/[p+k(1-p)]$ and $q_{\mathrm{no\ relief}}=kq_{\mathrm{relief}}$. The selective scenario uses $k=3$ in the novel group and $k=1$ in the standard group. One study generates patient outcomes and missingness indicators; repeated studies use mathematically equivalent multinomial counts for observed/missing outcomes with/without relief. Available cases are analyzed using the actual group sizes, the pooled score test without continuity correction, and Newcombe-Wilson intervals. Bias and coverage refer to the full recruited population difference. Unestimable comparisons are counted separately. Downloads record the scenario, recruitment count, loss assumptions, selection multiplier, population probabilities, repetition count, and random seed.

The calculations use R and the shared functions in `R/sample_size_functions.R`. The interactive R apps use Shiny and are distributed for the browser through Shinylive. R Markdown and Bookdown compile the tutorial. The [source repository](https://github.com/KataTam/sample-size-calculation) supplies the code and `renv.lock`, which records the project package environment.

For a reproducible record, your saved report should identify the actual R and relevant package versions used, the app or script, and the exact repository commit. A tutorial build and a browser app can use different R environments. The build information below describes this tutorial build; an app result should be documented using its own runtime information.

## Reproduce or adapt an example {#reproduce-or-adapt-the-examples .advanced-heading}

You can begin with [Activity: Simulate repeated chronic pain trials](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=pain_simulation). After running a scenario, you can save its replications and assumptions, study plan and R script using the lab's download controls. The script loads shared functions from a repository checkout, so that checkout's commit should be recorded alongside it.

A practical reproduction follows these steps:

1. The source checkout should match the recorded code version. Its documented environment should be restored before running the saved script.
2. Saved inputs should match the result being checked, including sample size, population assumptions, test settings and simulation repetitions.
3. The saved script should run from the repository root. Its summaries can then be compared with the exported result using unrounded values where available.
4. Any changed method, software version or assumption should be documented before interpreting differences in the output.

For a compact example of the binary repeated-study algorithm:

```{r algorithm, eval=FALSE}
# Load the tutorial's analysis functions from the repository.
source("R/sample_size_functions.R")
# Make the random draws reproducible when rerunning this script.
set.seed(20260921)
# B is the number of trials; n is the number of patients in each group.
B <- 5000
n <- 60
# Generate each trial's number with relief directly from a binomial distribution.
treatment_count <- rbinom(B, n, .60)
control_count <- rbinom(B, n, .30)
# Analyze each pair of group counts with the same test.
results <- analyse_binary(treatment_count, control_count, n, alpha = .05)
# Estimate power as the fraction of trials with p < .05.
mean(results$p_value < .05)
```

Adaptations should keep the editable R Markdown, shared case settings, app code and build instructions together. You should review changes to assumptions and methods alongside the resulting figures and activities. The [adaptation guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/adaptation_guide.html) provides practical steps [@bothmann2021].

## Your own study {#own-study .advanced-heading}

Your study report can include a simulation result with its generating assumptions, analysis, repetition count and Monte Carlo interval. Your explanation should address what it adds to the analytical calculation. You can also write a short hypothetical study abstract that distinguishes the planned design, realized results and interpretation, following the broader learning sequence used in DICE [@thiesmeier2024].

Your project may involve estimation, a fixed dataset or dependent observations. The [study-design guide](#study-designs) should inform your choice of method. In [Activity: Build your own study calculation](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/study/?activity=own_study), you can assess plausible assumptions and resource limits, then explain whether to proceed, collaborate, redesign or narrow the question. The [reproducibility record](#reproducibility-record) should accompany the result.



<div class="chapter-recap">

### Take-home points {.unnumbered}

- Computational reproducibility uses the same inputs and procedures; replication investigates the same question with new data.
- Software and its settings should match the planned analysis, including the meaning and units of each input.
- A calculation record should include assumptions, methods, results, rounding rules, and software and code versions.
- A simulation record also needs data-generating assumptions, the analysis, the number of repetitions, and random-number settings.
- Complex designs also need their success rule, interim and adaptation decisions, final analysis and dated protocol/SAP versions.
- Sharing protocols and code supports checking and reuse. Data access should respect consent, confidentiality and other applicable restrictions.

</div>

## About this resource {-}

This tutorial builds on Katalin Tamási’s original e-learning module [@tamasi2021]. Its presentation and three simulation activities draw on chapters 1, 11 and 15 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022]. Hans Burgerhof’s *Statistics 3: Sample size calculation* e-learning module informs the discussion of testing and estimation goals [@burgerhof2020], with further statistical background from @kirkwood2003, @whitley2002, @pourhoseingholi2013 and @wang2020.

Our account of developing the epidemiology and medical statistics e-learning environment describes the learner and teacher needs underlying this approach [@wieringa2025]. Evaluation emphasizes explanations, application to new cases, and usability feedback, since access counts and time online may not reflect learning [@chan2019]. The [teaching guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/TEACHING_GUIDE.html), [case template](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/case-studies/student_case_template.html) and [assessment rubric](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/teaching/assessment_rubric.html) support classroom use. The tutorial uses R Markdown [@allaire2021rmarkdown] and bookdown [@xie2021bookdown]; the build environment records the versions used for the current edition.

Except where otherwise noted, original teaching materials are shared under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) and original code under the [MIT License](https://opensource.org/license/mit). The [reuse and citation guidance](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reuse-and-citation.html) explains attribution and third-party exceptions. Shared adaptations of the teaching materials must use the same or a compatible license. Publishing student work, identifiable feedback, or named student acknowledgments requires consent.

## Further reading {-}

Your choice of reading can follow the decision you need to make; the [reading guide](https://katatam.github.io/sample-size-calculation/documentation/reading-guide.html) connects these sources to the activities.

- @fong2026 and @zrineh2026 introduce clinical planning; @lakens2022 explains alternative sample size justifications; @cook2018delta2 supports choosing and reporting a [target difference](#target-difference). Apply these to the assumptions report.
- Design-specific guidance: @ying2025 and @eldridge2016 address pilot objectives; @candel2023 addresses efficient designs; @riley2020 addresses prediction-model development. CONSORT's explanation and elaboration details reporting, including sample size assumptions in item 16a [@consortee2025].
- For multiple outcomes and testing hierarchies, see @fdamultiple2022. For interim analyses, stopping guidelines and sample-size re-estimation, see ICH E9, Sections 3.4 and 4.4-4.6 [@iche91998], and @fdaadaptive2019. These support the [testing strategies](#multiple-outcomes-comparisons) and [additional reporting checklist](#complex-design-record).
- For the distinction between an observed significance boundary and planned power, see @lakens2022 and section 1.7 of *Power Analysis with Superpower* [@superpowerbook2022]. Chapters 11 and 15 of that book extend the simulation examples.
- Advanced methods and reference books: @pargent2024 explains mixed-model simulation, and @superpowerbook2022 supports exploring repeated studies. @julious2004 reviews normal-outcome trial calculations; @julious2023 provides broader design-specific sample size methods. @piantadosi2024 places planning within broader trial methodology. These books offer further detail on design-specific methods.

For readers exploring prediction models, @shamsutdinova2026 describes recent simulation-based approaches (currently in preprint).

For specialized designs, @vembye2024 provides guidance and the POMADE R package for power analysis of meta-analyses with dependent effect estimates. @dey2026 develops calculations for sequential multiple assignment randomized trials (SMARTs) with skewed outcomes. These sources provide further reading on specialized designs. @marks2026 complements the Bayesian planning methods with evidence about their use and reporting in trials.
